ideas.solution: Ingest bids, extract every checkable claim (reference customers, uptime, certifications, incident history, prior contracts) and verify against public records, contract databases, court dockets, security advisories and automated outreach to references. Deliver a one-page evidence-scored comparison that the evaluation committee can attach to the award file.
ideas.why_now: The vendor-side tools (NationGraph raised $22.5M to help vendors read documents and write proposals) have collapsed the signal in bids. Michigan's fraud-system disaster ($20M settlement plus $78M replacement) has made buyers nervous.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-5K per RFP for small buyers, or annual subscription for a state or co-op ($25-100K). A per-audit fee for high-risk software and AI awards.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone is selling to the vendor who is writing. The scarce, budgeted, blame-averse buyer is the one drowning in identical documents and has no tool that raises the cost of lying.
ideas.first_30_days: Take five closed public RFPs and publish a teardown showing which claims failed verification. Offer free pre-award checks to 5 county procurement offices. Charge from the second use.

ideas.title: Gauntlet Rehearsal Range for Drone Startups
ideas.one_liner: A private test range that reproduces the Drone Dominance Gauntlet scoring so new entrants can rehearse, fail cheaply and qualify before the real event.
ideas.customer: Drone makers preparing for Gauntlet 2.5, 3 and 4, from Series A startups to hardware teams entering defense for the first time.
ideas.problem: In Gauntlet 1 only 24% of drones reached 10 km, and even in Gauntlet 2 only 11 platforms hit 15 km. Each event has a limited slot count, roughly 6 months apart. New entrants burn scarce runs discovering avoidable failures, and few have range access or scoring instrumentation.
ideas.solution: Lease land and airspace near a Front Range site and instrument it to the published Gauntlet metrics (range, sortie count, jamming, payload, ease of operation). Sell run-blocks with independent data logs, a failure-mode report and a readiness score.
ideas.why_now: About 60,000 drones will be ordered from winners, and the 200,000-unit target by 2027 pulls in dozens of new entrants. The Gauntlet cadence is public, and a wave of Gauntlet 2.5 bomber-drone entrants is forming now.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-25K per run-block, $60-120K seasonal packages, and a sponsor arrangement with primes or investors who want pre-screened suppliers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When a market runs on tournaments, the money goes to the rehearsal facility that every contestant needs. This is the pick-and-shovel of a public competition schedule.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish the Gauntlet 2 metrics as a public scorecard and lease a private test site with a landowner. Buy a few reference drones and a logging stack. Sell 3 startups a pre-Gauntlet 2.5 block.

ideas.title: Public-Records Vault for City Employee AI Chats
ideas.one_liner: Capture, retain, redact and produce every government employee's AI prompt and response as the public record it legally is.
ideas.customer: City clerks, county records officers and city attorneys at cities of 20-300K people that just rolled out AI assistants to staff.
ideas.problem: Every prompt and output from a government employee is likely a public record subject to retention schedules and open-records requests. Cities are turning AI on in Chattanooga-style rollouts with no retention system. A single request from a journalist could force manual digging through vendor logs the city may not control.
ideas.solution: Browser extension and API proxy that captures AI interactions across tools, tags them to retention schedules, redacts exempt content (personnel, law enforcement, attorney-client), and generates one-click productions for open-records requests. Litigation-hold support included.
ideas.why_now: Local AI adoption is now real, with police, school and bus-routing deployments. GenAI.mil users have built more than 100k agents. Records lawyers are starting to warn, and the first open-records fights over chatbot logs will land in 2026-27.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-40K per year per city by headcount, plus e-discovery production fees. Reseller channel via records-management vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: AI adoption creates a records problem before it creates a safety problem. The clerk, not the CIO, has a legal deadline and a small budget line for exactly this.
ideas.first_30_days: Talk to 10 city clerks and 3 state records associations. Build the capture extension for two chat tools and a retention-schedule mapper. Pilot free with 2 cities that have announced AI programs, and convert on the first open-records request.

ideas.title: Model-Swap Regression Service for Contractors
ideas.one_liner: Automated testing and porting that lets defense contractors re-platform their AI workflows to a different model vendor in weeks without losing quality.
ideas.customer: Defense integrators, primes' AI teams and mid-size government contractors whose workflows were tuned around one model family and must now change vendors.
ideas.problem: The D.C. Circuit upheld the DoD supply-chain-risk designation of one model vendor on Sept 26, and DoD is moving classified workloads off it by October. Contractors are cutting that vendor's use. Their prompts, agents and evaluation sets were tuned for one model, and nobody can prove a replacement performs equally on their real tasks.
ideas.solution: Capture the contractor's existing workflow traces, build a task-specific eval set, run it across Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok and open-weight models, and auto-rewrite prompts and tool schemas to reach parity. Deliver a signed parity report usable as evidence for the government customer.
ideas.why_now: The designation is a fresh legal fact with an October deadline. Vendor politics now shape the supply chain, and lawful-use terms differ by vendor. Model swapping is now a compliance event, not an engineering preference.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-200K per migration project, then $3-10K per month for continuous cross-vendor regression monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The designation is not a one-time event. Every future vendor dispute will force the same migration, so the durable product is a standing eval-and-port harness for a politically volatile model market.
ideas.first_30_days: Post a fixed-price migration audit at $15K. Contact 15 small integrators and GenAI.mil agent builders through defense AI communities. Reuse one eval harness across clients while keeping each client's data separate.

ideas.title: Secret-Shopper Audits of Government Algorithms
ideas.one_liner: Submit synthetic applicants and questions to public benefits systems, chatbots and eligibility tools to measure real error and denial rates, then sell the evidence.
ideas.customer: State auditors and legislative oversight offices, legal-aid funders, civil-rights litigators, and government AI vendors that want an independent seal before a contract renewal.
ideas.problem: State and local buyers cannot audit the AI they bought, and no one owns post-award monitoring. Michigan's fraud detector wrongly accused 40,000 people and cost $20M plus $78M for a replacement. Contracts run 7 years with only 3% of provisions covering cybersecurity.
ideas.solution: Run agent-driven synthetic-case testers against public-facing eligibility screeners, 311 and permit chatbots, and (with authorization) internal decision tools. Publish error-rate and disparity reports with reproducible test cases. Offer a continuous monitoring subscription to buyers.
ideas.why_now: Cities and counties have moved from pilots to production AI, and the Glass/Sourcewell marketplace pilot covers about 120 agencies. Agentic testers are cheap in 2026, and Michigan makes the harm undeniable.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-120K per audit engagement, $5-15K per month for monitoring, and grant-funded public-interest audits. Vendors pay for certified re-tests.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Public-interest audit funders and state auditors already have budgets and mandate but no measurement tool. The synthetic-case method needs no vendor cooperation and no data access.
ideas.first_30_days: Run a free audit of 10 public-facing city or state chatbots and publish the findings. Send the report to state auditors and legal-aid funders. Sign one paid audit from a funder or auditor.

ideas.title: Facility-Clearance-in-a-Box and Cleared Bench
ideas.one_liner: A facility-clearance sponsor plus a rentable bench of already-cleared engineers for the wave of newly funded defense startups winning first classified subcontracts.
ideas.customer: Series A-C defense startups and small business subcontractors with a first classified task order but no facility clearance or cleared staff.
ideas.problem: Defense startups raised $14.6B in five months of 2026, and awards are accelerating. Startups cannot sponsor clearances without a contract and cannot start work without cleared people. Sponsorship and adjudication take months, so classified work stalls and startups lose the window.
ideas.solution: A cleared small business holds the FCL and employs a bench of cleared engineers, program managers and security officers. It subcontracts them to startups by the hour, provides FSO services, and manages the startup's own path to clearance. Includes shared SCIF time at partner facilities.
ideas.why_now: Record capital plus fast-lane vehicles (Megatron IDIQ, the Space Force valley-of-death office, Navy marketplaces) create hundreds of first-time classified subcontractors at once. Federal staff shortages mean primes want ready capacity.
ideas.revenue_model: Cleared-labor margin (25-40% on $150-250 per hour), monthly FSO retainers ($4-10K), and SCIF seat fees. A roll-up of small cleared staffing shops adds scale.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Cash is no longer scarce for defense startups, but time-to-cleared-work is. The binding constraint has moved from funding to a slow, government-controlled credential that can be rented.
ideas.first_30_days: Acquire or partner with a small cleared firm that already holds an FCL. Recruit 5-8 cleared freelancers and retired government staff. Pitch the 20 most recently funded startups and place the first two engineers.

ideas.title: Blue UAS Bill-of-Materials Origin Auditor
ideas.one_liner: Part-by-part origin verification so 60,000-drone orders do not fail on hidden Chinese-origin motors, radios and cameras.
ideas.customer: Drone makers and their integrators selling to DoD and public safety, and the primes that must certify their subcontractors' parts.
ideas.problem: Compliance requires proving that components meet domestic-content and ownership rules, but sub-tier motors, ESCs, batteries and cameras often trace to opaque distributors. Manufacturers self-certify with spreadsheets and hope a re-labelled part is not found mid-contract.
ideas.solution: Upload a BOM and receive origin confidence per part. Cross-check import records, distributor invoices, factory databases and optional lab teardown or spectrum fingerprinting of sample units. Deliver an auditor-ready dossier and alerts when a supplier changes source.
ideas.why_now: Drone Dominance orders make component provenance a gating item for tens of thousands of units. About 48 defense firms are IPO candidates and want clean compliance records. Gauntlet winners must scale quickly and can't afford a failed audit (verify statutory citations).
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25K per BOM audit, $2-8K per month for monitoring, and per-sample teardown fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not certification but suppliers' unofficial data. Trade-data analytics plus teardown labs beat legal-only compliance firms because they can catch a repackaged part.
ideas.first_30_days: Audit 3 drone BOMs for free to build a dataset. Hire a customs-data analyst and a contract RF engineer. Pitch Gauntlet participants directly.

ideas.title: CMMC Enclave for CNC Shops
ideas.one_liner: A prebuilt, shop-floor-aware CUI enclave and evidence pack that gets 20-person machine shops through CMMC Level 2 without rebuilding their IT.
ideas.customer: Job shops and small manufacturers making parts for defense primes (castings, forgings, machined parts), roughly 30,000-plus firms in the defense supply base.
ideas.problem: CMMC Level 2 assessments for contract awards ramp up from Nov 2026 (verify dates). Shops keep CUI drawings on machine-side PCs and USB sticks, and generic CMMC consultants scope the entire company. Sub-tier suppliers lack IT staff and capital, exactly the bottleneck AIA-Bain describes.
ideas.solution: A managed enclave that isolates only the CAD/CAM and CNC controllers handling CUI, ships as a pre-configured appliance plus cloud tenant, and comes with policies, evidence collection and assessor liaison. Fixed monthly price, no consultants hourly.
ideas.why_now: Phase-in of the CMMC rule puts assessment on contracts through 2026-27, and primes are pushing flow-down requirements. Sub-tier financing is scarce, so shops need a low-capex option.
ideas.revenue_model: $800-2,500 per month per shop plus $5-15K onboarding. Channel through primes who will subsidize their suppliers' compliance.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Scope reduction is the whole business. The winning product understands machine tool OT and draws a tight boundary around it, while horizontal CMMC vendors sell a heavy enterprise program.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 shops through a regional manufacturing extension partnership. Assemble the appliance from commodity parts. Sign one prime's supplier program as channel.

ideas.title: Grant Recovery Desk for Small Cities
ideas.one_liner: A contingency-fee grant compliance and reimbursement service for small cities receiving FEMA, DOJ and counter-drone money with no staff to document it.
ideas.customer: Towns and counties with populations of 5-100K, especially those receiving disaster reimbursements and new safety grants (for example the $500M FEMA counter-UAS program).
ideas.problem: Small governments lose federal reimbursements to incomplete documentation, procurement missteps and audit findings. With federal agencies shrinking and reorganizations stalled in court, help is thinner. Dallas County is cutting IT staff, and local budgets are tight.
ideas.solution: A software-plus-service program that structures the grant lifecycle: eligibility check, procurement compliance, receipt capture, quarterly reporting and closeout audit packages. It uses AI to read award terms and flag non-compliant purchases before they happen. Paid from recovered funds.
ideas.why_now: New grant streams (counter-drone, cyber, disaster) are landing at localities while federal grant-management staff are being cut. Regulators enforce documentation harder as budgets tighten.
ideas.revenue_model: Contingency of 4-8% of recovered or protected award dollars, with a minimum retainer. A city with $2M in awards yields about $80-160K.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer pays nothing up front, and the alternative is losing money already awarded. Contingency pricing turns a dreaded compliance cost into free money for a small clerk's office.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer free award-file reviews to 10 small cities identified from public award lists. Build a compliance checklist per program. Sign 2 contingency deals.

ideas.title: Accessible Council Packets Pipeline
ideas.one_liner: An automated pipeline that makes every agenda packet, staff report and PDF a city publishes accessible on arrival, ahead of the ADA Title II deadline.
ideas.customer: City and county clerks and IT directors in jurisdictions above 50,000 residents (deadline April 26, 2027), then smaller ones (2028).
ideas.problem: Cities publish thousands of legacy PDFs, scanned minutes and meeting packets that fail web accessibility rules. Manual remediation costs $3-10 per page and lawsuits are coming. Staffing is thin, and the deadline is fixed.
ideas.solution: Connect to the city's agenda-management and document repository, auto-remediate PDFs (tags, reading order, alt text, tables), route low-confidence pages to human reviewers, and enforce accessible-by-default templates for future documents. Provide the compliance log a city attorney can cite.
ideas.why_now: ADA Title II rules set April 2027 for larger jurisdictions and 2028 for smaller ones. GenAI makes remediation of complex documents cheap enough to price against manual work.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-80K per year per city depending on volume, plus a backlog cleanup fee ($20-100K one-time).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The recurring stream of new weekly agenda packets, not the legacy backlog, is the durable business. Ship the pipeline at the moment of publishing rather than a one-time remediation project.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape 20 city websites and score their accessibility publicly. Offer free packet remediation for the next council meeting to 5 clerks. Convert on the backlog cleanup quote.

ideas.title: CJIS 6.0 Identity Kit for Small Agencies
ideas.one_liner: A managed multifactor and identity-verification stack that works in patrol cars, radio dead zones and shared workstations, ready for the Oct 1, 2027 CJIS deadline.
ideas.customer: Sheriff's offices and police departments with 10-150 sworn officers and no dedicated IT security staff, plus the managed service providers that serve them.
ideas.problem: CJIS 6.0 requires MFA and identity verification by Oct 1, 2027. Generic MFA breaks on shared terminals, offline vehicles and old mobile data computers. Small agencies buy compliance piecemeal from a few vendors and fail audits.
ideas.solution: Hardware keys plus a cached-token offline mode and a shared-workstation login flow, with an agency-level compliance dashboard and audit-ready evidence. Onboard officers in minutes through mobile driver's license or badge-based identity proofing.
ideas.why_now: The deadline is fixed and less than 13 months out. Agencies are starting budget cycles now, and state CJIS systems agencies will begin enforcing.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-15 per user per month or a per-agency package of $6-30K per year, plus hardware sold at cost plus margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the MSP serving 50 small agencies. One channel partner delivers dozens of deployments, and offline behavior is the differentiator that enterprise identity vendors will not build.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2 MSPs that serve sheriffs. Prototype offline token caching on a rugged laptop. Run 3 no-cost pilots in agencies with upcoming CJIS audits.

ideas.title: Offline Distilled Agent Box for Denied Networks
ideas.one_liner: Ruggedized GPU box that runs small models distilled from a unit's own GenAI.mil agents, with zero connectivity.
ideas.customer: National Guard and reserve units, Army and Marine tactical staffs, border and disaster-response agencies, and defense integrators serving units in disconnected or denied environments.
ideas.problem: GenAI.mil is unclassified only and needs connectivity, yet users built more than 100k custom agents. The CDAO says compute is the binding constraint, and classified models cannot train in commercial data centers. Units in the field cannot use any of it.
ideas.solution: A service that takes a unit's approved agent workflows on GenAI.mil, distills them into small open-weight models with tool wrappers, and ships them on a rugged 1-2 GPU box with a one-screen interface. It updates by sneakernet with signed model bundles.
ideas.why_now: Open-weight small models are now good enough for narrow tasks. Right-sizing to cut inference cost is an explicit DoD priority, and model-vendor politics make owning a portable, vendor-independent model attractive.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-90K per box and $2-5K per month for update and distillation services. Government pilot funding via SBIR or CSO awards.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The 100k user-built agents are an unwritten requirements document for what warfighters want. The winner distills the demand signal, not the model.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask 3 Guard units for one repetitive workflow (maintenance triage, reporting). Build a demo on commodity hardware with an open-weight model. Apply for one SBIR topic and ask an integrator for a paid subcontract.

ideas.title: Passive-Radar Drone Detection for Prisons
ideas.one_liner: Detect small drones by listening to ambient cell, broadcast and Wi-Fi signals, with no transmitter, no license and no radar permit.
ideas.customer: State departments of corrections, county jails, and secondary customers such as critical infrastructure and stadiums.
ideas.problem: Cape Canaveral radars see aircraft up to a 747 but not a quadcopter. State prisons face contraband drops with low budgets and cannot deploy active radar or jammers. Remote ID and RF detection miss drones that are not broadcasting.
ideas.solution: A rooftop kit of low-cost software-defined radios using the signal reflections of existing cell towers and broadcast transmitters, with ML-based detection of small-drone Doppler signatures. It alerts a mobile app and logs evidence for prosecution, and it is passive so legal risk is minimal.
ideas.why_now: Cheap SDRs and modern ML make passive sensing of low-cross-section targets feasible in 2025-26. Small-drone detection is now flagged as thin even at major federal sites, and drone traffic is exploding with 200,000-unit purchases (verify feasibility and prison contraband scale).
ideas.revenue_model: $25-60K per site installation plus $500-1,500 per month for software and monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Passivity is the business model. Local agencies cannot legally emit RF or mitigate, so a purely receiving sensor is the only kind they can buy without federal permission.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit one university RF lab. Pilot on a rooftop with an existing tower nearby and log real drone passes. Approach 3 state corrections security chiefs for a paid pilot.

ideas.title: Magnetic Maps for GPS-Denied Drone Navigation
ideas.one_liner: A data company that maps low-altitude magnetic anomalies and sells the layers that let cheap drones navigate without GPS.
ideas.customer: Drone makers and integrators in Drone Dominance and Navy autonomy programs who need GPS-denied performance, and later defense agencies seeking quantum navigation.
ideas.problem: Jamming defeats GPS, and magnetic navigation needs detailed low-altitude field maps. Public datasets are coarse, and hardware teams do not want to become mapping companies. The Navy is asking for quantum navigation and degraded-environment navigation.
ideas.solution: Fly survey drones carrying vector magnetometers over test ranges, training areas and border regions, publish tiles through an API, and provide a reference navigation filter that drone makers can integrate. Start with the Gauntlet region and US test ranges.
ideas.why_now: Cheap, sensitive magnetometers and onboard compute make magnetic navigation practical for small drones. Fleets of attritable drones can also continuously enrich the map. The Navy calls for quantum and degraded-network navigation (verify map resolution claims).
ideas.revenue_model: Per-area annual licences ($20-100K per region), per-tile API access, and custom survey work for programs. Defense SBIR funding for range expansion.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The map, not the sensor, is the moat and it compounds. Every drone that flies with a magnetometer improves the map, so the mapping firm becomes the network owner.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy two survey rigs and map one test range and one agricultural area. Publish accuracy results. Offer 3 Gauntlet participants a pilot navigation filter and tile access.

ideas.title: Sub-Tier Surge Twin for the Industrial Base
ideas.one_liner: A digital twin of foundries, forges and motor makers that shows which supplier breaks first in a 180-day fight.
ideas.customer: Defense primes' supply-chain risk teams, private equity funds rolling up defense suppliers, DoD industrial-base offices, and sub-tier lenders.
ideas.problem: Leaders doubt they can sustain the 90-, 120- or 180-day fight and lack integrated supply-chain visibility. AIA-Bain identifies castings, forgings, sensors, semiconductors and solid rocket motors as bottlenecks. Private equity invests only $1-3B a year and is flying blind on capacity.
ideas.solution: Build a network model of sub-tier capacity from public and commercial data (facility permits, trade flows, workforce, energy use, certifications), calibrated by supplier surveys. Run agent-based surge scenarios to identify chokepoints and invest-or-acquire targets. Start with one commodity, castings and forgings.
ideas.why_now: The record defense funding wave is looking for bottlenecks to fund. Maven-scale AI targeting has raised concern about munition depth. Agentic simulation and cheap data enrichment make a 5-person twin feasible.
ideas.revenue_model: $60-250K per year per subscribing prime or fund, plus deal-sourcing fees on roll-up acquisitions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The people who will pay first are private equity funds hunting acquisition targets, not the Pentagon. The twin's early output is a target list for whoever wants to roll up the base.
ideas.first_30_days: Map 300 casting and forging plants from public data and publish a bottleneck brief. Present to 5 PE funds and 3 primes' supply-chain teams. Sign one paid pilot for a commodity view.

ideas.title: Proof-of-Resident Public Comment
ideas.one_liner: Privacy-preserving verification that a public comment or 311 report comes from a real resident, without collecting their identity.
ideas.customer: City clerks, county boards, school districts, planning departments and state agencies running public-comment portals.
ideas.problem: Governments use GenAI to write documents, and vendors and activists use AI to flood the channels back. Councils and agencies can no longer tell 50 real residents from 5,000 bot-generated comments, so legitimate voices lose weight and hearings are contested.
ideas.solution: A comment widget that accepts a zero-knowledge proof from a mobile driver's license or wallet credential, proving residency and unique personhood without revealing name or address. Public dashboards show verified versus unverified counts, and the clerk keeps an audit log.
ideas.why_now: Mobile driver's licenses are live in a growing number of states, and wallet-level zero-knowledge proofs shipped in 2025. The signal-to-noise collapse from AI-generated submissions is now visible in procurement and public comment.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-30K per year per jurisdiction, with per-verification fees for state agencies and rulemaking dockets. Partner with agenda-management vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Verification without identity is the only approach that a hostile public will accept. Councils do not want a citizen database, they want a trustworthy count.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the widget with an open wallet-credential library in a state that supports mobile IDs. Pilot with one city clerk for a controversial hearing. Publish the verified-versus-unverified result.

ideas.title: Seasonal Staff Housing from Banned Rentals
ideas.one_liner: Master-lease flats stranded by short-term-rental bans and sublet them by the bed, with employer-guaranteed rent, to short-staffed hotels in the same destination.
ideas.customer: Hotels, resorts and restaurant groups with 50-400 seasonal staff in Palma, Ibiza, Barcelona coast and similar hotspots (start in the Balearics). Secondary customer: small owners whose licences are ending.
ideas.problem: Insiders frame STR bans as residents versus tourists, with owners as the losers. The overlooked fact is that banned owners have empty flats and fear 12-month tenancy law, while the hotel next door cannot hire because staff cannot find housing. Nobody sits in the middle to handle leases, furnishing, inspections and deposits.
ideas.solution: An asset-light intermediary signs 6-11 month leases with owners under a structure vetted by local counsel. The hotel guarantees the rent and places its own staff. We handle furnishing, house rules, inspections and optional payroll-deduction of rent, and charge per bed. The wedge is one Palma pilot with 3 hotels and about 30 flats.
ideas.why_now: Palma has a full ban, Barcelona bans all STRs in Nov 2028 after Spain's top court upheld it in Oct 2025, and Madrid restricts listings. Spain fined Airbnb $75M in Dec 2025, so the stranded supply is real. Spain still had about 97M visitors, so hotels are staffing to record demand.
ideas.revenue_model: A 12-18% management fee on rent, or a EUR 40-70 per bed per month spread, plus a placement fee from the hotel and a fee for guaranteeing rent to the owner.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A ban strands supply as well as demand, and the best tenant for that supply is the employer of the people who service tourism. Employer-guaranteed rent is better credit than any nomad or mid-term tenant, which lets owners accept lower rents for zero vacancy risk.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact HR and operations heads at 15 hotels through the Mallorca hoteliers' federation and LinkedIn, and sign 3 letters of intent for 10-20 beds each. Recruit 30 owners through ex-STR property managers and owner groups. Pay a local lawyer EUR 3-5K for a lease template. Sign leases only after the hotel LOIs are in.

ideas.title: Parking-Slot Gates for Overrun Villages
ideas.one_liner: Sell tiny hotspot villages and trailheads a plate-recognition parking and coach-slot reservation system whose price rises until arrivals fit a hard cap.
ideas.customer: Municipalities, mountain and coastal park authorities and private lot operators in places like Alpine lake villages, Dolomites passes, Cinque Terre-type towns and Croatian or Greek islands. Budgets are under EUR 50K, and they already own parking revenue.
ideas.problem: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, because a small flat fee is dwarfed by trip cost. Open villages cannot install turnstiles, but almost every day visitor arrives by car, coach or shuttle. Those arrival modes are countable and enforceable, and nobody prices them dynamically.
ideas.solution: A cheap camera and plate-recognition kit plus a web app. Visitors reserve parking and coach slots at prices that rise with demand until the cap holds. Residents and overnight guests are exempt through a plate allow-list synced from hotels' check-in data. The cap becomes a subsidy for staying overnight.
ideas.why_now: Edge computer vision and plate recognition are now cheap. Record arrivals (1.52B international in 2025) and visible failures of flat fees have made mayors ready to try hard caps. Mount Fuji's 4,000/day cap plus fee shows caps are politically acceptable, and a few Alpine lakes already require reserved road access in peak season.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS of EUR 300-900 per month per site, plus 3-5% of slot fees collected, plus a hardware lease.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Price the arrival mode rather than the person. Cars and coaches are the physical valve for day-trip load, and exempting overnight guests turns a congestion rule into a booking incentive that local hotels will help sell.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 3 villages that already have paid lots. Run a manual pilot with a reservation page and a phone-camera plate check by a local attendant, with no hardware. Sign private lot operators first, since they can decide fastest. Ask mayors for a summer 2027 pilot and a letter of support.

ideas.title: Advance Hotels Their Stuck OTA Payouts
ideas.one_liner: A neutral lender advances 90-95% of completed-stay OTA payouts on checkout day for a flat 1.5-2% fee, so independent hotels stop financing the OTAs.
ideas.customer: Independent hotels and small groups of 20-150 rooms in Europe with 60-80% of bookings through Booking.com, Expedia or Agoda.
ideas.problem: Insiders treat OTA payment collection as a convenience. In practice about 70% of Booking Holdings' 2025 bookings used its payment service, and hotels are paid after checkout. That is weeks of float while they pay staff, energy and suppliers at costs that have repriced sharply since the Hormuz shock. Banks cannot see these receivables, so nobody underwrites them.
ideas.solution: Read reservation and payout schedules from the hotel's channel manager or extranet export. Underwrite each receivable, which is checked out and has a scheduled payout from a top-three OTA. Advance the cash the same day, and sweep repayment when the OTA pays. Later, extend to advances on confirmed future stays for seasonal cash needs.
ideas.why_now: OTA merchant payments became the majority path in 2025. Energy and construction costs repriced after the March 2026 Hormuz closure, and capital is described as disciplined and selective. Open banking and embedded-finance rails make small-ticket receivables lending workable for a small team.
ideas.revenue_model: A 1.2-2.5% fee per advance, which is about 20-40% annualised on 2-4 week paper, funded by a credit-fund warehouse line, with a small servicing fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The merchant model quietly turned hotels into unpriced lenders to OTAs. A checked-out receivable from a top-three OTA is close to risk-free collateral that has never been packaged, because lenders cannot see reservation-level data.
ideas.first_30_days: Line up EUR 300-500K from a specialty credit fund or family office. Recruit 5 independent hotels through revenue-management consultants and hotel associations. Offer to advance manually against payout statements they email, testing repayment on the next OTA payout before building any integration.

ideas.title: Resident Proof for Two-Tier Tourist Pricing
ideas.one_liner: A privacy-preserving QR proof of residence lets towns, museums and transit charge visitors more and locals less without building databases or discriminating by nationality.
ideas.customer: Municipalities and municipal attractions, ferries and parking in overrun towns of 5-100K people (Italy, Croatia, Spain, Japan), then private attractions and restaurants offering locals-first pricing.
ideas.problem: Insiders think dual pricing is a legal and PR minefield, useful only in niche places. It is spreading (reported moves include Rome's charge for non-resident visitors at the Trevi Fountain and resident-versus-visitor pricing at some Japanese castles). The real bottleneck is verification. Each site checks IDs by hand, builds a one-off app or discriminates crudely.
ideas.solution: Issue a wallet pass from the municipal residents' register, first over the town hall counter and later through national digital-ID wallets. It discloses only 'resident of X'. Gates and apps verify it offline, and the same pass unlocks locals-first booking windows and discounts. The town gets analytics on non-resident flows to tune fees.
ideas.why_now: Venice's flat fee reportedly did not reduce numbers, so cities are turning to differentiated pricing. EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by the end of 2026, which makes selective-disclosure credentials mainstream. Resident backlash is at its peak.
ideas.revenue_model: Municipal SaaS of EUR 10-30K per year, EUR 0.01-0.05 per verification, and an integration fee per attraction.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Pricing policy is not the bottleneck; identity is. Whoever standardises the 'resident' claim owns the tollbooth for every future visitor-management rule, including resident-first windows, non-resident caps and local discounts.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach one town of 5-20K people that runs a municipal attraction, ferry or car park. Offer a free 90-day pilot where staff issue passes at the town hall and verify them with phone cameras. Use mayors' associations to find the pilot, and have a lawyer confirm the residency-based structure is proportionate.

ideas.title: Convert Empty Thai Hotel Floors to Monthly Stays
ideas.one_liner: Take under-filled floors of mid-tier Thai hotels on revenue share and run them as furnished 30-90 day remote-worker wings, replacing lost Chinese group demand with sticky monthly stays.
ideas.customer: Owners of 80-300 room three- and four-star hotels in Bangkok, Phuket, Pattaya and Chiang Mai whose Chinese group volume collapsed. End users are remote workers, retirees and long-stay sports or wellness visitors.
ideas.problem: Thailand's 2025 arrivals fell 7.2% and sit 17% below 2019, with Chinese arrivals down 33.5%. Insiders wait for Chinese groups to return, but Chinese outbound is shifting to independent travellers who go farther and spend less on hotels. Empty floors bleed fixed costs, while nomads on 40+ visa schemes struggle to find reliable monthly stays.
ideas.solution: We take 20-40% of rooms and add a coworking corner, bonded fast internet, laundry, community events and monthly billing. Guests pay USD 650-1,100 per month including utilities, for a 30-day minimum. We market through nomad communities and groups and help with long-stay visa paperwork. The hotel keeps F&B upside.
ideas.why_now: The China demand collapse leaves stranded capacity. Thailand's long-stay Destination Thailand Visa exists for remote workers, and 40+ countries now offer nomad visas. Nomad information is now free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so operators win on product, not discovery.
ideas.revenue_model: A 20-30% management fee on room revenue or a fixed lease spread, plus ancillary revenue from SIMs, insurance and visa-service referrals.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Hotels are optimised for nights while nomads buy months. A floor at 90% occupancy on monthly rates beats 35% occupancy at full nightly rates, and monthly guests do not pay 22-28% OTA commission.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 2 hotels in Bangkok or Chiang Mai on a 60-day trial of 10 rooms each. Build a one-page site and post in nomad and expat groups. Target 15 monthly bookings, and record occupancy and revenue per available room against the hotel's nightly baseline.

ideas.title: Hotel Strike Early-Warning for Event Planners
ideas.one_liner: A subscription database and parametric cover that tells meeting and group planners which contracted hotels' labour contracts expire before their event, and pays out if a strike hits.
ideas.customer: Association and corporate meeting planners, incentive houses, sports and event organisers and tour operators that contract 100+ room-night blocks 12-24 months ahead.
ideas.problem: Chicago hotel workers authorised a strike at 85%, potentially the largest in the city's history, and a Seattle Hilton strike lasted 85 days. Planners contract blocks years ahead and learn about labour risk from the news. Strike coverage under contract clauses is vague, and relocating an event on short notice costs heavily.
ideas.solution: Track union contract expirations, strike votes and bargaining status per property, from union pages, filings and news. Score each hotel and date for strike risk, alert planners, and provide a labour-disruption clause template. Later add parametric cover underwritten by an MGA that pays per room-night if a strike affects a contracted property.
ideas.why_now: Hotel labour unrest is elevated in 2026, hotel costs have repriced sharply, and hotel operators are cutting staff citing AI (Mews cut 15%). Planners are more exposed to relocation than ever.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 3-8K per year per planning team, cover premiums of about 1.5-3% of block value, and broker fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A strike is a scheduled event, not a surprise. Contract expiry dates are public, yet the buyers of long-dated blocks bear the tail risk and nobody prices it.
ideas.first_30_days: Compile a spreadsheet of union contract expirations for the top 40 US convention cities from union local sites and news. Publish a free '2027 events at risk' report to planner communities, then convert responders to a USD 2K annual subscription. Line up an MGA for the cover after the first 10 customers.

ideas.title: City Micro-Rule API for Group Tour Operators
ideas.one_liner: A continuously updated database of group caps, loudspeaker rules, coach drop-off bans, fees and overnight-parking bans across overtouristed places, delivered as an itinerary checker for tour operators and campervan renters.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size group tour operators, DMCs, shore-excursion companies, guide associations and campervan or RV rental firms in Europe.
ideas.problem: Cities answer overtourism with many small rules, such as group-size caps and loudspeaker bans in places like Venice and Amsterdam, plus coach access fees and wild-camping bans elsewhere. These live in local-language ordinances, and fines fall on operators and guides. Nobody publishes a single source of truth.
ideas.solution: Use multilingual LLM ingestion of municipal ordinances with human legal review for the top 60 cities. The product is an itinerary checker that flags violations and fees, a weekly change digest, an API for booking systems and a WhatsApp bot for guides.
ideas.why_now: Municipal crackdowns keep multiplying (Barcelona, Palma, Venice, Amsterdam, the Balearics, Glasgow's levy from Jan 2027). Long-context LLMs make parsing ordinances in many languages cheap only recently.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 79-299 per month per operator, enterprise API licences for cruise lines and campervan renters, and paid city packs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Overtourism policy has fragmented into thousands of tiny local rules. The pain is compliance risk rather than any single rule, and every new rule makes the product more valuable.
ideas.first_30_days: Curate rules for 10 cities (for example Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Dubrovnik, Lisbon, Athens, Edinburgh and Kyoto) with local guides. Sell 10 operators at USD 99 per month through guide associations, and publish free rules-by-city pages for SEO lead generation.

ideas.title: Work-From-Abroad Compliance Ledger for Employers
ideas.one_liner: A Slack-native ledger that tracks where remote employees actually work and flags tax, payroll, permanent-establishment and visa thresholds before 30 days from Lisbon becomes a liability.
ideas.customer: Remote-first companies with 50-1,000 employees, their HR and finance teams, and the tax advisors who serve them.
ideas.problem: Over 40 countries have nomad visas with thresholds from under USD 1,000 to over USD 7,000 per month, and some ban local employment. The EU Entry/Exit System has tracked non-EU travellers' 90/180-day stays automatically since April 2026. Employees informally work abroad, and companies do not know their exposure. Consumer trackers show individuals their days but give employers no aggregate view or approval flow.
ideas.solution: An opt-in ledger built from calendar entries, flight emails and optional device location, with a rules engine per country (183-day tests, 90/180 rules, permanent-establishment risk days, social-security thresholds, nomad-visa work rules). Employees request a workation, get an auto-check, then a manager approves. Export an evidence pack for tax advisors.
ideas.why_now: EES is fully live since April 2026, nomad visas keep multiplying, tax authorities are tightening, and return-to-office fights push employees to work from abroad informally.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 4-8 per employee per month with a USD 2K annual minimum, plus advisor referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the employer holding the liability, not the nomad. Information is free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so value has moved to compliance evidence and approval workflow.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 20 HR leads at remote startups through remote-first communities. Build a Slack bot that answers '/workation Lisbon 6/1-6/30' with rules for 10 countries. Charge a flat USD 150 per month and partner with 2 international tax firms.

ideas.title: Verified Cool-Night Rooms for Heat-Stressed Europe
ideas.one_liner: Cheap in-room sensors prove a hotel room stays below about 26C at night, sold as a certificate, a refund guarantee and a machine-readable rating for booking agents.
ideas.customer: Hotels, B&Bs and STR operators in Greece, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Portugal and Turkey, with OTAs, agent builders and insurers as secondary buyers.
ideas.problem: Summer heat makes 'air-conditioned' meaningless, since old units, weak cooling and poor insulation leave rooms hot at night. Nobody measures indoor night temperature, so complaints turn into refund disputes. Rerouted demand into Turkey and Southern Europe, and a focus on 'value for money', make heat a rising complaint.
ideas.solution: Fit a USD 10-15 wireless sensor per room in about 10 minutes. It logs a nightly indoor temperature curve, and we issue a 'Cool Night verified' certificate showing the share of nights below the threshold, with a public verification page and JSON feed for AI agents and metasearch. Hotels also get a dashboard to find and fix problem rooms, and can add a hotel-funded heat refund guarantee.
ideas.why_now: Repeated European heatwaves, cheap connected sensors, and AI booking assistants that need structured, verifiable attributes because star ratings and 'AC yes/no' are uninformative. Booking's commoditisation of listings makes measured differentiation valuable to independents.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 6-9 per room per month, a EUR 150 install kit, an annual certification fee, and data licensing to platforms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Comfort is the one hotel attribute that is physically measurable yet almost never measured. In a world of agent-driven booking, a verified physical attribute becomes a ranking signal.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 hotels in Athens, Crete, Sicily and Puglia using off-the-shelf sensors. Offer a free 30-day 'truth test' and publish an anonymised heat report for press. Convert 10 to paid subscriptions.

ideas.title: Guardrail Gateway for Hotel AI Agents
ideas.one_liner: A proxy between hotel AI agents (voice, chat, booking) and PMS, POS and door-lock APIs that enforces per-action permissions, spend limits and human approval for irreversible actions.
ideas.customer: Hotel AI vendors that need enterprise trust, hotel groups' IT and security teams, and cyber insurers.
ideas.problem: Hotels are deploying agents fast (Dextr AI raised a USD 6.7M seed for hotel voice agents on 24 Sep 2026, and 109 AI use cases have been catalogued across 39 hotel systems). Practitioner commentary warns agents often hold API access built for trusted staff, so a prompt-injected guest message could trigger refunds, comps, rate changes or key issuance. PMS platforms have no concept of a scoped agent identity.
ideas.solution: An API and MCP gateway in front of PMS platforms (start with one that has a public API). It is read-only by default, applies caps on write actions (small refunds auto-approve, larger ones go to staff for approval in Slack or WhatsApp), redacts personal data, has a kill switch and keeps immutable logs. It ships with a red-team pack of injection attacks.
ideas.why_now: Agents are moving from pilots to production in 2026, PMS vendors are opening APIs, and agent protocols such as MCP are mainstream. Insurers and enterprise buyers are starting to ask for controls.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 49-149 per property per month, OEM licences to AI vendors, and insurer referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In the agent gold rush the scarce item is the permission model, not the agent. AI vendors will pay for it as a sales enabler, and insurers will pay because it caps their loss.
ideas.first_30_days: Build against one PMS with a public API (Mews or Cloudbeds). Sign 2 hotel AI startups as design partners, and publish a red-team report showing injection weaknesses in demo agents (with permission) to earn press and inbound interest.

ideas.title: Contingency-Fee Audit of OTA Markups and Payouts
ideas.one_liner: Mystery-shop every downstream reseller and reconcile every OTA payout, then take a share of the money and direct bookings recovered.
ideas.customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms and small groups in Europe and the US paying 15-28% commissions.
ideas.problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate, up from 40% two years ago, and 26% do not know whether rates are passed on. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA, Southwest and loyalty partners are invisible to rate-shopping tools. Hotels are paid after checkout, and commission, virtual-card fee and no-show errors go unchecked. In-house monitoring exists for chains (Radisson watches 1,600 properties), but independents have nothing.
ideas.solution: Combine automated and human shoppers that check rates across OTAs and reseller portals with screenshots per date, and reservation-level reconciliation of booked rate, commission, payout, card fees, cancellations and no-shows. Produce evidence packs to send to OTA account managers and a price-integrity dashboard that supports the case for direct booking.
ideas.why_now: Booking's payment service touched about 70% of its 2025 bookings, which concentrates the opacity. Google AI Overviews now reportedly show hotel prices and cut metasearch clicks, which pushes hotels to defend direct channels. Channel managers now expose reservation data.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-25% of recovered commission and no-show revenue, plus USD 99-299 per month for ongoing price-integrity monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: OTAs cannot audit themselves and hotels cannot see downstream markups, the same structural gap that made freight-bill and telecom-audit firms lucrative. The shopping evidence is the leverage in negotiations.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer 20 hotels a free 'leak report' covering 30 future dates, using human plus scripted shoppers. Convert the worst-leaking ones to contingency contracts, using hotel associations for introductions.

ideas.title: Visitor-Levy Back Office for Councils
ideas.one_liner: White-label registration, returns, audit and enforcement software plus a service desk that lets local councils run a new tourist levy without building it.
ideas.customer: Local authorities that have just gained the power to levy visitors: Scottish councils, Welsh councils, and Spanish, Balearic and other European municipalities.
ideas.problem: Levies are proliferating (Edinburgh in 2026, Glasgow from Jan 2027, Welsh councils from 2027, Balearics and Catalonia rising, Chicago at 19% hotel tax). Each council must register providers, collect returns, audit and chase non-payers, and most have neither software nor staff. Small B&Bs and self-caterers file badly and disputes pile up.
ideas.solution: A packaged portal for provider registration and returns, with support for per-night and percentage levies, exemptions, OTA-collected amounts and platform data feeds. It includes automated reminders, audit sampling, a provider help desk and a statutory report pack, configured per council within weeks.
ideas.why_now: New statutory levies start across the UK through 2026-27, and EU short-term rental rules require platforms to share host data with authorities from May 2026. That data can be matched against levy returns. Councils' levy revenue lets them fund administration.
ideas.revenue_model: GBP 20-60K per council per year, or a share of collected levy, plus per-return service fees for the help desk.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Levies fail on administration rather than on rate-setting. Every council needs the same back office at the same moment, and levy revenue pays for it, so the customer has a budget line before it has a system.
ideas.first_30_days: Talk to 10 councils and the Welsh and Scottish local-government bodies. Offer a fixed-fee pilot of a provider portal and returns form for one small council. Build it from a form tool and a database first, then harden.

ideas.title: Extranet Takeover Defense for Independent Hotels
ideas.one_liner: Managed monitoring and fraud response for hotels' OTA extranet logins and guest-messaging channels, the credential theft that turns into guest payment scams.
ideas.customer: Independent hotels, B&Bs and small STR managers of 10-150 rooms, their channel-manager and PMS resellers, and cyber insurers.
ideas.problem: Attackers phish or infect front-desk staff, take over OTA extranet accounts and message arriving guests from the genuine booking thread asking for payment via fraudulent links. The hotel absorbs chargebacks and reputational damage and can lose OTA account standing. These hotels have no IT staff and are too small for security vendors.
ideas.solution: A light service that watches for leaked credentials tied to the hotel's domain and staff emails, alerts on suspicious extranet login emails, flags guest messages containing external links or payment requests, and runs 10-minute staff phishing training. It adds a 24/7 hotline for incident response and a guest-facing 'how we ask for payment' page.
ideas.why_now: AI-written phishing in dozens of languages, widely reported hospitality-targeted credential theft campaigns in 2025, and merchant-model payments that concentrate risk in OTA accounts. Insurers are hardening cyber requirements.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 49-149 per property per month, insurer commissions and per-incident response fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The weak node is the hotel's front-desk laptop, not the OTA platform. The unit of attack is a booking thread the guest already trusts, so simple detection at the message level gives most of the protection.
ideas.first_30_days: Run a free credential-exposure scan for 100 hotel domains using public breach data. Send each hotel its results, convert 10 to paid, and partner with two hotel associations for distribution.

ideas.title: Accessibility Disclosure Kit for US Independent Hotels
ideas.one_liner: A phone-based room-measurement kit that produces the accessibility details federal law requires on booking pages, before serial plaintiffs sue.
ideas.customer: US independent hotels and small groups of 30-300 rooms, franchisees, and the ADA-defence law firms who refer them.
ideas.problem: The federal hotel reservation rule (28 CFR 36.302(e)) requires booking systems to give enough detail about accessible rooms for guests to judge suitability, yet most sites just say 'ADA room'. Serial-filer suits repeat across the same properties and cost thousands each to settle. AI booking assistants also need structured answers on step-free showers and bed heights.
ideas.solution: A staff app guides a 20-minute walkthrough per room type using phone measurement and photos (door widths, turning space, shower type, bed height, grab bars). It generates compliant descriptions and a structured feed for OTAs, Google and AI assistants, then monitors listings for drift and provides a litigation-readiness pack.
ideas.why_now: Hotels are now being listed in AI assistants that demand structured attributes, and phones with depth sensing make measurement cheap. Serial-filer litigation continues, which gives the wedge and the budget.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 600-1,500 one-time per property plus USD 25-60 per month for monitoring, with rev-share to referring law firms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit gets you the budget and the structured data is the moat. Detailed accessibility data is the missing input for agent booking, and accessible travel is an underserved segment.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2 ADA-defence firms. Run a free scan showing what a serial filer sees on 100 hotel websites as lead-gen, and sell a USD 499 audit to 20 properties.

ideas.title: Package Travel Surcharge Compliance for Tour Operators
ideas.one_liner: A rules engine that calculates lawful fuel-driven price increases on already-sold package tours, generates the notices and tracks the 8% cancellation trigger.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size EU and UK package organisers, coach-tour and cruise-package sellers, and agents acting as organisers with EUR 5-200M in sales, plus their bonding insurers.
ideas.problem: With the Hormuz closure and soaring jet fuel, packages sold months ago are underwater and airlines are cutting capacity and raising fares. Under EU and UK package rules an organiser can raise prices only if the contract allows it, only for fuel, tax or exchange-rate changes, with at least 20 days' notice, and an increase above 8% lets travellers cancel free. Organisers must also pass on decreases. Spreadsheet errors mean refunds and regulator complaints.
ideas.solution: Connect to booking exports, model the cost components per trip, compute the lawful pass-through per contract clause, and generate localised notices with timelines. Track the 8% threshold and deadlines, keep an audit trail for regulators and bonding insurers, and flag contracts whose clauses need rewriting.
ideas.why_now: Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed on 2 Mar 2026 and, by September, budget carriers cite soaring fuel costs with capacity cuts and fare hikes ahead. Shorter booking lead times (33 days versus 37.5) do not help packages sold long in advance.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per operator or about 0.1% of sales, plus per-notice fees and clause redesign consulting.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a cost shock much of the loss is legal rather than commercial. Operators eat costs because they misread pass-through limits or send defective notices, so compliance software turns panic into recovered margin.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a calculator and notice templates in a spreadsheet plus an LLM. Publish a gated '2026 fuel surcharge playbook' through trade associations, and sell 10 operators at EUR 500 per month.

ideas.title: Overtourism Feed for AI Travel Agents
ideas.one_liner: A destination-signed, machine-readable feed of live capacity, closures and dispersal incentives that AI trip agents query, so places can steer planning before tourists arrive.
ideas.customer: Destination management organisations and city tourism boards in overtouristed regions (Balearics, Dolomites, Kyoto, Lisbon, Dubrovnik, Amsterdam), later transport agencies and hotel groups.
ideas.problem: AI agents now plan and book trips (Booking.com and Expedia apps run inside ChatGPT), and they recommend the same hotspots blind to caps, closures and crowding. DMOs intervene only after arrival with fees and fines, which Venice's reportedly ineffective day-tripper fee shows is weak. Referral traffic from search is being eaten by AI answers.
ideas.solution: Publish an MCP server and JSON feed per destination with a daily load index by place and hour (from ticketing, parking, cruise calendars and occupancy), hard caps and permits, equivalent alternatives within about 60 minutes with partner lodging, resident-first hours and off-peak incentive codes. DMOs get a dashboard showing how many agent-planned trips shifted. Start with a hosted API and a DMO-embedded chatbot for immediate use.
ideas.why_now: OTA apps are now inside AI assistants, MCP servers are mainstream, booking lead times are shrinking, and AI overviews reportedly cut metasearch clicks by 31% in tested markets. DMOs need a way to influence the plan rather than the queue.
ideas.revenue_model: DMO subscriptions of EUR 20-100K per year, transparent sponsored 'dispersal' placements paid by under-visited partners, and analytics.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Overtourism control is an information-timing problem. Influence must happen at itinerary generation, and AI agents are the first chokepoint where a single feed can shape millions of itineraries, giving destinations robots.txt-style power.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a feed for one region from public data (cruise schedules, park permit status, museum time slots) and ship the MCP server. Offer 3 DMOs a free traffic dashboard as design partners and embed it in their own website chatbots. Approach trip-planner app builders for consumption.

ideas.title: Book the Unbookable: Agents for Offline Suppliers
ideas.one_liner: A voice-and-WhatsApp agent phones, negotiates and confirms bookings with small inns, guides and boat operators that have no API, then turns each one into bookable inventory.
ideas.customer: Independent travel advisors and small DMCs first, later AI trip-planning apps and OTAs seeking long-tail inventory.
ideas.problem: The best small inns, agriturismi, ryokan, guides and boat operators take bookings by phone, WhatsApp or email in local languages, with deposits by bank transfer. Advisors spend hours per booking, AI agents cannot book them and OTAs do not list them. Hotel-side voice AI is crowded (for example Dextr AI's seed), but buyer-side is empty.
ideas.solution: A real-time multilingual voice and text agent calls or messages the supplier, checks availability, negotiates a net rate within the advisor's limits and sends the deposit. A human verifies the money step. Every completed booking builds a structured supplier profile (hours, languages, deposit rules) that becomes API-bookable next time.
ideas.why_now: Real-time voice models now handle 30+ languages, WhatsApp Business is universal, and agentic payment tooling exists. Shrinking booking lead times and rerouted travel create demand for fast alternatives beyond OTA inventory.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 20-60 or 3-5% of booking value per booking from advisors, SaaS for DMCs, and later a take rate from suppliers and inventory data licensing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Long-tail supply is invisible to agents because it lacks an API, not because it lacks quality. The cheapest API is a phone call made by a machine with a human closing the money step, and each call builds an inventory graph nobody owns.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick Japan, Italy and Greece. Recruit 15 independent travel advisors and process 100 bookings semi-manually with human voice operators shadowing the agent at USD 30 per booking. Measure time saved and conversion.

ideas.title: Trust Oracle for Rental Listings and Agents
ideas.one_liner: An API that answers whether a vacation rental exists, is legally registered and is controlled by the host, so payment firms, insurers and AI booking agents can refuse scams.
ideas.customer: Payment providers handling travel, travel insurers, villa-rental agencies and AI trip-agent developers, later consumers via a plug-in.
ideas.problem: AI-generated photos and cloned listings fuel rental fraud, and agents will soon book unattended. The EU short-term rental regulation requires registration numbers from May 2026, but there is no cross-border way to verify them and each registry differs. Bans (Barcelona 2028, Palma) will also see illegal listings delisted at the last minute, stranding guests.
ideas.solution: Aggregate public registries (Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, France, NYC and others), geocode the address and match it to satellite and street imagery, reverse-search photos and detect duplicates. Return a verified, unverified or unregistered verdict with evidence in under two seconds, as an API and an agent tool.
ideas.why_now: Registry numbers make 'is it legal' a lookup for the first time, agentic booking needs automated trust, and AI imagery has broken manual checks. Enforcement is rising (Spain's USD 75M fine on Airbnb).
ideas.revenue_model: USD 0.05-0.50 per check, USD 2-10K per month enterprise plans, and a share of insurer premiums saved.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Registration numbers convert legality from opinion into data, and agents cannot get a bad feeling about a listing. Whoever builds the legality and fraud graph first becomes infrastructure for every automated booking flow.
ideas.first_30_days: Build for Spain, Italy and Portugal using public registers. Offer a free check widget to villa agencies, and backtest known scam cases to pitch two travel-insurer fraud teams.

ideas.title: One Guide, Twelve Languages: Live-Dubbed Tours
ideas.one_liner: The guide speaks once and each guest hears their own language in low-latency synthesised audio, so mixed-language groups share one guide and cities see fewer, fuller groups.
ideas.customer: Independent guides, small tour operators and shore-excursion companies in cities that cap groups (Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Kyoto), plus guide associations and municipalities.
ideas.problem: Language-siloed tours multiply the number of groups on the same street, and group-size caps and guide quotas bind. Guides cannot fill rare-language tours, and whisper systems only amplify the guide's voice.
ideas.solution: Guide microphone to live speech translation to each guest's phone, joined by QR with no app install, with per-listener language choice, a glossary of place names, an offline fallback, headcount tools and translated questions back to the guide. Sell a clip mic and hub kit plus per-tour credits.
ideas.why_now: Real-time speech-to-speech translation became good enough in 2025 (consumer earbuds now offer live translation and APIs offer realtime speech), eSIM and 5G make connectivity easy, and cities are tightening group caps.
ideas.revenue_model: USD 39-99 per guide per month or USD 1-2 per guest, USD 150 kits and municipal licences.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Language silos are a hidden multiplier of overtourism. Merging groups cuts the number of groups without cutting visitors, so guides earn more and cities become allies and customers.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 20 guides in Rome and Florence, pilot two-language tours then four, and measure latency and guest satisfaction. Approach the guide association with the pilot results.

ideas.title: Wildfire Evacuation Autopilot for Campsites and Hotels
ideas.one_liner: Satellite fire-spread alerts plus pre-contracted buses, routes and multilingual guest messaging turn every tourist lodging in fire country into an evacuation node.
ideas.customer: Campsites, holiday parks and hotels in fire-prone Mediterranean regions (France's Aude, Var and Gironde, Catalonia, Greece, Portugal, Croatia), plus regional tourism boards and insurers.
ideas.problem: Summer wildfires now force sudden evacuations of thousands of tourists who have no local knowledge, often no cars and no shared language. Duty of care sits with small operators holding paper plans they have never drilled, while insurers tighten terms.
ideas.solution: A site-specific evacuation plan with two routes and a refuge, ingestion of hourly fire detections (NASA FIRMS, Copernicus EFFIS and commercial satellite feeds), wind-aware fire arrival estimates per site, and automatic guest alerts by WhatsApp or SMS in the guest's language using check-in data. It includes a staff checklist and drills, and standby contracts with local coach operators.
ideas.why_now: Higher-frequency satellite fire detection arrived with early-2025 launches such as FireSat, and wildfire seasons in 2025 were severe across Southern Europe. Insurers and regulators are pressing small operators.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 300-1,200 per site per year, margin on coach standby retainers, insurer premium-discount share and regional government contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Tourist lodging is the largest concentration of people in fire zones with no local knowledge, no vehicles and no common language, and the legal duty sits with operators who cannot afford risk consultants.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 25 campsites in Aude, Hérault, Var and Gironde through the camping federation. Deliver a plan PDF and WhatsApp alerts at EUR 390 per year, run one drill and pitch two insurers with results.

ideas.title: Paid Holds: Options Market for Booking Agents
ideas.one_liner: A merchant plugin that sells time-limited holds on appointments, tables and inventory to shopping and booking agents, so agent traffic becomes fee revenue for the merchant instead of something to block.
ideas.customer: Wallet-holding consumer assistant agents and browser agents, which pay through AP2, ACP or Stripe/Tempo MPP rails. Supply side is independent restaurants, salons, dentists, physios, tee-time, boat and experience operators on Acuity, Square Appointments, Booksy, Cal.com or Mindbody.
ideas.problem: Agents shop in parallel. One errand fans out to 20-50 merchants and the agent wants to keep the best option open until its principal approves. Free holds are free options, so merchants see phantom demand, no-show slots and sold-out tables. Their response is to block agents: eBay barred buy-for-me agents in Feb 2026 and Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent on 22 Sept 2026.
ideas.solution: The merchant sets a hold price (for example 2-5% of ticket value, $1 minimum) and a duration (10 minutes to 24 hours). The agent calls hold(), pays programmatically and gets a signed hold receipt the merchant honors. If the agent converts, the fee is credited to the booking. If not, the merchant keeps it and we take 25%. The service also dedupes so retrying agents don't double-book. Later, hold prices float with demand, giving each slot an implied option value.
ideas.why_now: Google's AP2 v0.2 added human-not-present payments and moved to the FIDO Alliance. Stripe and Tempo's Machine Payments Protocol went live in March 2026, and Visa and Mastercard both have agent rails. Merchants are blocking agents right now, and the Ninth Circuit vacated Amazon's injunction against Perplexity in Aug 2026, so blocking is legally shaky. Visa expects millions of agent-made purchases this holiday season.
ideas.revenue_model: 25% of hold fees, plus a 1-2% referral fee on converted bookings. The merchant plugin is free to install. Later, a paid demand-analytics dashboard for merchants showing agent search intent by slot.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Merchants are not hostile to agents. They are hostile to free options. Agents are the first buyers rational enough to price optionality, so charging for holds turns an adversarial scraping problem into a market. Airlines already sell fare holds, so the concept is proven with humans. Agents make it viable at $1 scale, and the hold price becomes a demand signal merchants have never had.
ideas.first_30_days: Build on the public webhooks and APIs of Cal.com, Acuity and Square Appointments. Recruit about 40 independent salons, barbers and physios in one metro with a free plugin, paying them out of our own test agents' wallets. Ship an MCP server exposing hold_and_book. Get 3 consumer-agent or browser-agent builders to integrate through x402/MPP hackathons. Measure hold-to-book conversion and no-show reduction, then charge live fees in months 2-3.

ideas.title: Waze for Agents: Live Bureaucracy Route Data
ideas.one_liner: A pay-per-lookup feed of the current, tested state of consumer and government web procedures (form changes, outages, hidden requirements, real step timings), sold to browser agents just before they attempt an errand.
ideas.customer: Browser and computer-use agents, and the agent platforms that run them, paying $0.005-$0.10 per route lookup via x402 or MPP. The heaviest users will be agents doing errands: license renewals, permits, benefits applications, insurance claims, utility transfers, refunds.
ideas.problem: Procedure websites change weekly with no changelog. Every failed attempt burns tokens, and worse, can leave a half-finished irreversible state such as a submitted but unpaid renewal. Every agent relearns the same breakages, and nobody pools that knowledge.
ideas.solution: Two data engines. First, synthetic canaries: daily automated dry-runs of the top ~500 US flows (state DMV and DOL, county property tax, SSA/IRS/USCIS account setup, top utilities, top insurers' claim portals, airline refund forms). They record schema diffs, required documents, CAPTCHAs, session timeouts and upload limits, and publish step-by-step 'route cards' with a success rate and freshness timestamp. Second, opt-in failure telemetry from customer agents, traded for credits, which covers the long tail Waze-style. Customers get a 'route guarantee': if a route verified in the last 24 hours fails, the lookup is refunded.
ideas.why_now: Browser agents moved from demo to production in 2026, with vendors reporting thousands of automated workflows per week on legacy portals. x402 and MPP make $0.01 lookups collectable without accounts. Governments are still not publishing agent-readable metadata.
ideas.revenue_model: Metered lookups, plus $500-$5,000/month platform plans for agent vendors that include telemetry credits. Premium verified-fresh routes for high-stakes flows, and later aggregate breakage analytics sold to agencies who want to fix their own forms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For an agent the scarce input is not information but freshness plus negative results: knowing what broke this morning. Agents' own failures are the raw material, so each new customer improves the map, a data network effect a static scraper cannot copy. Government sites are the one part of the web nobody will ever optimize for agents, which keeps the drift problem permanent.
ideas.first_30_days: Write 50 Playwright canaries for the 10 highest-traffic flows in 5 large states, using a cheap model to diff DOM and field schemas. Publish a free MCP server and a public 'status page for bureaucracy' to draw agent builders. Offer free credits to 5 browser-agent startups in exchange for telemetry, and start charging in month 3 once the route guarantee has a track record.

ideas.title: Clickwrap Gatekeeper: Agents Buy Contract Counsel
ideas.one_liner: An API agents call before clicking 'I agree'. It returns clause-level risk against the principal's delegated-authority policy, plus a signed archive of exactly what was accepted.
ideas.customer: Wallet-holding consumer and enterprise agents, and the platforms that run them, paying $0.02-$0.50 per document evaluation plus an evidence-archive fee per acceptance. Agent-wallet and browser-agent vendors are the natural embedders.
ideas.problem: Agents will accept tens of thousands of ToS, DPAs, auto-renewals, arbitration waivers and data-resale clauses for people and companies. Courts increasingly treat automated assent as binding, so the open legal question is the scope of the agent's authority. Agents can read a contract, but none has a legal-grade policy engine or a defensible evidence trail. Amazon's fight with Perplexity over agent access is one visible example of that unsettled authority.
ideas.solution: check(url_or_text, policy) diffs the document, hash-cached and versioned, against the principal's policy: max liability, no auto-renew beyond 30 days, no mandatory arbitration, no resale of personal data. It returns ALLOW, ESCALATE or REFUSE with cited clauses. On ALLOW it snapshots the page (hash, timestamp, screenshot) into a tamper-evident log so the principal can later prove what was accepted. A diff feed alerts the principal when terms change on services already accepted. It is positioned as a policy engine, not legal advice, with law-firm-authored policy packs.
ideas.why_now: Agent authority is the live legal question of 2026, with law-firm memos on 'authority to bind' and litigation over agent access. Payment protocols such as AP2 mandates and ACP mean agents now click through payment terms without a human present. Browser agents are in production use.
ideas.revenue_model: Metered evaluation (first-seen documents priced high, cache hits nearly free), an evidence-archive fee per accepted contract, enterprise policy packs, and a marketplace for lawyer-written policy templates with a revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The unit of legal risk in the agent economy is not the model's hallucination but the tiny irrevocable assent. Because most ToS are near-identical templates, one shared cache amortizes legal analysis across millions of agents, which no single company can do for itself. Lawyers become policy authors rather than reviewers, and gross margin exceeds 90% once the cache is warm.
ideas.first_30_days: Crawl and index ToS, privacy and DPA pages for the top 5,000 SaaS and e-commerce sites and cluster them into templates. Publish a free MCP server with 1,000 free checks. Recruit 3 advisory lawyers to seed policy templates. Pitch agent-wallet startups and browser-agent vendors to embed it as a pre-payment check, and start charging in month 2.

ideas.title: Escrow Notary for Agents Hiring Humans
ideas.one_liner: A neutral adjudication layer that agents pay per task to verify that a hired human really did the physical job before escrow releases, built to withstand AI-forged proof.
ideas.customer: AI agents and orchestrators that hire humans for physical tasks (pickups, in-person checks, photographs, errands) through RentAHuman-style boards or MCP gig APIs. They pay $0.50-$3 per verification plus 3-5% of escrow on disputes. Marketplaces themselves are a second buyer.
ideas.problem: An agent cannot see reality and is easy to fool. Generated photos are good enough that a picture is no longer proof. RentAHuman launched in Feb 2026 with MCP integration and large sign-up numbers, but researchers found that tasks stalled, payments errored and visible supply was thin. Neither the agent nor the marketplace wants the cost of verification.
ideas.solution: A verification bundle priced by task value. Evidence is captured in a signed app (C2PA-style provenance, device attestation, liveness, GPS and time, and a random challenge such as 'show today's code next to the item'). Tier 1 is automated checks. Tier 2 is an independent 'witness' (a second human or a fixed camera or sensor). Tier 3 is human adjudication. The result is a signed attestation the agent's escrow contract accepts to release funds. Fraud fingerprints are pooled across every marketplace served.
ideas.why_now: Agent-hires-human marketplaces exist and are growing. Generative fakes broke photo-as-proof. Stablecoin escrow through x402 or MPP makes conditional release trivial to automate.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-verification fee ($0.50-$3), 3-5% of escrow value on adjudicated disputes, a platform contract with marketplaces, and later an insured 'completion guarantee' priced from the pooled fraud data.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In agent-to-human labor the scarce thing is not labor supply but trust in evidence, because the buyer cannot look. Verification is a cost center no marketplace wants to build and every agent needs, so a neutral notary can sit between marketplaces the way escrow.com sat on top of eBay. The cross-marketplace fraud graph becomes the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a free verification app and an MCP tool verify_task(task_id, evidence). Recruit ~200 witnesses in 3 cities. Pilot with two agent-errand marketplaces and five indie agent developers who hire humans for local pickups, at $1 per verification. Publish anonymized fraud statistics to establish credibility.

ideas.title: Recipient-Priced Inboxes for Outbound Agents
ideas.one_liner: A gateway that lets busy people set a price to reach them and makes outbound AI agents bid for attention, refunding the bond when the message proves relevant.
ideas.customer: Outbound agents (fundraising, PR, recruiting sourcing, partnership and research-interview agents) that decide per message whether a reply is worth $1-$50 and pay a refundable bond. The recipient side is VC partners, journalists, podcast bookers, specialist physicians and procurement heads.
ideas.problem: Agents remove the cost of sending, so high-value inboxes are drowning. Generic AI outreach now gets under 1% replies in most B2B segments, and reaching one buyer takes 7+ touches. Filters are an arms race, and recipients earn nothing for their attention.
ideas.solution: The recipient sets a price ladder (for example $5 for a read-guarantee, $25 for a reply window) and rules. Unknown senders get an auto-reply, or an HTTP 402 for agents, carrying a payment link. The sender agent estimates expected value from its own conversion data and posts a refundable bond over MPP, x402 or card.
