Build a simple three-scenario model and publish a free index and a short note. Send it to 50 muni credit analysts and airport finance officers and sell the first five paid subscriptions.

ideas.title: Work-Share Desk: Kurzarbeit for American Employers
ideas.one_liner: Administer state short-time compensation for mid-size employers so they can cut hours 20-40% instead of laying off skilled staff, with workers drawing pro-rated unemployment benefits.
ideas.customer: Employers with 50-800 employees (manufacturers, distributors, engineering firms, PEO-served businesses) in states with work-share programs, buying through the CFO, HR head or PEO.
ideas.problem: Roughly 33 states have short-time compensation programs, yet take-up is tiny because employers do not know they exist and the paperwork (plan applications, weekly certifications, state-specific rules, payroll integration) is painful. Layoffs then destroy trained staff who cost one to two times salary to replace when demand returns.
ideas.solution: A layoff-versus-work-share calculator for CFOs, plus a done-for-you service. It checks eligibility, prepares the state plan, connects payroll (Gusto, ADP, Rippling) to generate weekly certification data, provides employee communication scripts and tracks the effect on the employer's unemployment account. Expand state by state and through PEOs and manufacturers' associations.
ideas.why_now: The oil shock (crude above $100, diesel near $6) and the September 2026 Fed hike, the first since 2023, are cooling consumers. Unemployment is still low at about 4.1%, so executives want to keep hard-to-replace workers and are wary of repeating the 2022-2023 layoff-then-rehire cycle.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 setup fee plus $10-15 per participating employee per week, or 15% of verified savings versus layoff and rehire. PEO channel revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The program exists but nobody built the admin layer because the payoff only arrives in downturns. This is a business that sells the same product every recession and can build its state-rule database and PEO channel during the quiet years. Retention value is high precisely because the labor market is still tight.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two manufacturing-heavy states with simple program rules (for example Ohio, Michigan or Pennsylvania). Publish a free layoff-versus-work-share calculator. Pitch 30 manufacturers via associations and PEOs and sign 5-10 at a $1,500 flat setup fee, doing the paperwork by hand at first.

ideas.title: Closing-Time Recovery for Shutting Small Businesses
ideas.one_liner: A contingency-fee agent that finds and collects the money owners forget when they close: tariff refunds, overpaid taxes, insurance returns, deposits and vendor credits.
ideas.customer: Owners of small businesses closing or filing Chapter 7 or Subchapter V (restaurants, boutique importers, e-commerce brands, agencies), plus trustees and wind-down lawyers who will not chase small assets.
ideas.problem: Exhausted owners walk away from uncollected money. Customs owes about $166B in IEEPA tariff refunds to roughly 330,000 importers after the Supreme Court struck the tariffs down on February 20, 2026, with refunds running through CBP's CAPE portal and protest windows expiring on a rolling basis. Beyond tariffs, there are overpaid sales and payroll taxes, unearned insurance premium, utility and landlord deposits, vendor credits, customer deposits, workers' comp dividends and unclaimed property. Trustees often skip small claims because the cost outweighs the return.
ideas.solution: Run a standard 40-item recovery checklist automatically: pull entry data through a licensed customs-broker partner with a power of attorney, search unclaimed property, send insurer audit and refund requests, and file claims with a partner wind-down attorney. Find leads from PACER filings, state dissolution records, lien releases, landlords and accountants. Take 20-30% of recovered funds and pay nothing if nothing is found.
ideas.why_now: Tariff refunds are moving but the deadlines to claim them are rolling off. Higher rates, the energy shock and squeezed lower-income consumers are pushing more small businesses to close. Contingency-fee legal and customs partners are available and CBP now has a digital claim channel.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered amounts, with typical finds of $8-40k per closing business. Referral fees from trustees and lawyers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The biggest asset in a dying small business is often not equipment but claims against governments and vendors the owner does not know exist. A closing owner has no bandwidth, so willingness to hand over a percentage is high, and the funnel widens in every downturn.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one wind-down attorney and one customs broker. Pull recent Chapter 7 and Subchapter V filings of importers and closed restaurants and send 300 letters offering no-win-no-fee reviews. Target 10 signed engagements and use the first recoveries as case studies.

ideas.title: Percentage-Rent Rails for Small Retail Strips
ideas.one_liner: Sales-linked leases with rent automatically swept from the tenant's POS, so independent landlords can fill dark restaurant and shop spaces and tenants stop dying under fixed rent.
ideas.customer: Owner-operator landlords of neighborhood retail strips and mixed-use buildings with vacancy, and independent restaurants and retailers seeking space. Platform revenue comes from landlords and processed rent.
ideas.problem: Higher rates and a squeezed consumer are closing independents. Landlords face 6-12 months of vacancy and costly tenant improvements. Percentage-rent leases align risk, but small landlords do not trust tenants' sales reports, so the structure has been confined to big malls.
ideas.solution: A standard 'base plus percent' lease template (a lower base of about 50-60% of market plus 5-8% of gross sales above a breakpoint). Rent is computed and swept automatically from Toast, Square or Clover data with tenant consent, and the landlord sees a live dashboard. Add leasing and brokerage, and a lender-facing cash-flow report so landlords can refinance on more predictable income.
ideas.why_now: Refinancing at higher rates pushes landlords to prefer occupied space. Rates just rose again and the consumer is K-shaped. POS APIs and embedded payments now make sales reporting verifiable and rent collection automatic for small operators.
ideas.revenue_model: 1-2% of rent flow processed, a leasing commission on placements, and a lender-reporting subscription. Optional financing spread for landlords.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Percentage rent died in small retail because of an information problem, not an economics problem, and POS data solves the information problem. Because landlord income scales with tenant sales, the system flips the landlord from adversary to partner and wins in booms as well as downturns.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit three landlords with vacant restaurant or retail spaces in one metro. Have a lawyer draft the lease template. Build Toast and Square OAuth plus ACH sweeps with existing tools. Sign two tenants on sales-linked leases and use their first rent runs as proof.

ideas.title: Mid-Term Premium True-Down for Shrinking Payrolls
ideas.one_liner: Monitor payroll against the estimate on a small business's workers' comp and liability policy, and file mid-term endorsements to cut inflated installments and misclassified codes.
ideas.customer: Small businesses with 10-200 employees and volatile payroll (trades, restaurants, staffing, light manufacturing) that already run payroll on Gusto, ADP, Rippling or QuickBooks, reached through CPAs and bookkeepers.
ideas.problem: Workers' comp and general liability premiums are priced on estimated payroll and revenue, and only reconciled at year-end audit. When headcount drops, the business keeps paying installments on inflated estimates, financing the insurer, often through premium finance at rising interest. Class-code misclassification (office staff coded as field staff) is also common. Brokers are paid a percentage of premium, so nobody is paid to lower it mid-term.
ideas.solution: Connect payroll data, compare actual payroll by class code with the policy estimate each month, generate the carrier endorsement request and support documents, and track the reduced installment schedule. Audit class codes and prepare audit-ready records. Offer optional pay-as-you-go workers' comp placement later.
ideas.why_now: Hiring freezes and layoffs are rising as the economy cools. Higher rates raise the cost of premium financing and make cash tighter. Payroll APIs are mature enough to automate the variance check.
ideas.revenue_model: 20% of the first-year realized premium reduction, or $49-99 per month SaaS. Partnerships with CPA firms and bookkeepers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The blocker is incentives, not technology. Brokers earn commission on premium, so no one in the chain is paid to file the endorsement. Downturns make the savings largest exactly when cash is scarcest.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 small businesses through two CPA or bookkeeper networks. Review each policy's declarations page against the last three months of payroll. File endorsements and misclassification challenges by hand, record the realized savings and set pricing at 20% of the first-year benefit.

ideas.title: Distributor Credit Radar for Failing Restaurants
ideas.one_liner: A weekly early-warning score on each restaurant account, built from public signals and distributors' own order and payment data, so food distributors can tighten terms before the customer goes dark.
ideas.customer: Independent foodservice distributors (produce, protein, dairy, beverage, paper) with $20-500M in revenue that sell on net-14 and net-30 terms to restaurants. The buyer is the credit manager, controller or owner.
ideas.problem: Restaurants are high-turnover, thinly capitalized credit risks, and distributors are unsecured creditors who see the problem last. Generic credit bureaus are weak on restaurants. When consumer spending is squeezed and rates are higher, bad debt climbs and distributors respond with blunt tools (COD for everyone) that lose good accounts.
ideas.solution: A risk score per account, refreshed weekly, combining health-inspection trends, permit and liquor-license status, lien and judgment filings, review and hours changes, delivery-platform activity, foot traffic, and the distributor's own signals (order-size decline, days-to-pay drift). Alerts recommend cutting limits, switching to COD or accelerating collection. A consortium data pool of anonymized payment experience improves the score for every member. A bad-debt shield insurance product can follow.
ideas.why_now: Squeezed lower-income consumers, higher borrowing costs and the energy-cost shock raise restaurant failures. Public and alternative data on restaurants is now cheap to assemble, and distributors are digitizing accounts receivable and order data.
ideas.revenue_model: $600-2,500 per month per distributor by account count, plus consortium data access and later an insurance referral share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Restaurants fail visibly weeks or months before they stop paying. The best predictor is the distributor's own order-size decline, which they are not analyzing, and the consortium effect (shared payment behavior) becomes a data moat no single distributor can build.
ideas.first_30_days: Get three regional distributors to share two years of anonymized accounts-receivable history and back-test whether public signals warn 8-12 weeks before write-offs. Sell a paid pilot at $1,500 per month. Each avoided $20k write-off pays for the subscription for a year.

ideas.title: Human Viva Examiners for AI-Wary Universities
ideas.angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
ideas.one_liner: A per-student oral-defense service where trained examiners in Nairobi, Manila and Chennai run 12-minute recorded vivas on submitted essays and code, giving US professors human-verified authorship evidence for about $10 a student.
ideas.customer: Writing-program directors, department chairs and online-degree program managers at US community colleges and mid-size universities (intro composition, intro CS, gateway business courses). Individual adjuncts with discretionary budgets are the first buyers. Admissions offices reviewing flagged essays come second.
ideas.problem: Harvard data from Sept 2026: 89% of professors received suspected AI work, 67% say AI hurts their courses, and only 12% referred cases to the honor council. Detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers. Nobody has the time or the standing to test an accusation, and a professor cannot personally hold 60 oral exams per section.
ideas.solution: The instructor uploads submissions and a rubric. The platform drafts 4-6 questions specific to each student's own paper. AI writes the questions but never judges. A vetted examiner in a matching time zone runs a 12-minute live video viva, scores it against the rubric, and marks the student as able or unable to explain their own work. The instructor gets a one-page evidence summary and the recording within 48 hours. Examiners are ex-teachers and graduate students who pass a 6-hour certification, and 10% of vivas are double-scored for QA. Students consent through the syllabus, and the institution signs a FERPA school-official agreement.
ideas.why_now: Faculty AI distress peaked in Sept 2026. NYC and LAUSD paused classroom AI for 2026-27, so 'human-verified' is now politically favored over AI-judging-AI. Proctored math accuracy has fallen from about 80% to about 60% while unsupervised work looks better. Meanwhile English-fluent graduates in Kenya, the Philippines and India face a shrinking entry-level BPO ladder, so a large trainable labor pool is available at $15/hour.
ideas.revenue_model: $9-14 per viva billed to the department, with examiners paid about $4-5 per viva (roughly $15/hour), for a gross margin near 55%. Departments can buy an annual site licence of $3-10k. An appeal viva is a $25 add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not detection, it is credible human attention. Detectors create accusations nobody can test, while a viva turns an accusation into an assessment: if the student can defend the paper, they learned it, however they drafted it. The only way to supply cheap, trusted, trained human minutes at scale is emerging-market labor, and the only buyers who will pay are institutions that just lost faith in remote work.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit and train 15 examiners through two teacher-training colleges or alumni groups in Kenya and the Philippines. Offer three community-college composition instructors a free 30-student pilot and record what share of students cannot explain their own paper. Charge $300 for the next batch, and reach instructors through adjunct communities and online-program managers. Run it on Zoom, a calendar tool and Airtable, with no custom platform until 10 paying sections exist.

ideas.title: Closed-School Science Labs Shipped to African Schools
ideas.angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
ideas.one_liner: Take decommissioned lab benches, microscopes, fume hoods and Chromebooks from US schools being closed, refurbish them into container-sized lab packages with a practical-exam curriculum, and sell them to private secondary schools in East and West Africa.
ideas.customer: Buyers are private and faith-based secondary school networks in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and Ghana, paying $8-15k per lab package. Sellers are US districts, charters and private schools that are closing and want fast, lawful disposal at low cost.
ideas.problem: More than 1,000 US public schools closed in 2025-26. Chicago alone has 135k empty seats, and Portland, Minneapolis and Albuquerque are queued behind it. Districts dispose of equipment through slow public-surplus auctions that recover pennies. Meanwhile African private schools running on tiny per-student budgets cannot afford lab equipment, even though national practical exams and newer competency-based curricula require it. A new lab costs $30-50k and takes months to import.
ideas.solution: Inventory soon-to-close buildings and remove complete science rooms, robotics kits, libraries and tested Chromebooks (with NIST-grade data wipes and export of working goods only). Bundle them into a 40-foot container with local installation, a practical-exam curriculum (matched to Kenyan, Nigerian or Ghanaian exam boards), a one-day teacher orientation, and a small annual refill of consumables. The district gets a disposal certificate and a possible donation receipt.
ideas.why_now: Closures are at a four-year high, so supply is predictable and geographically concentrated. The AI memory crunch, with memory now 30-40% of a device's bill of materials, has raised new-device prices and made used Chromebooks valuable. Distributed solar and batteries mean African schools can now run lab equipment and computers. As I understand it, Kenya's first competency-based senior-school cohort (2026) requires STEM practicals many schools cannot deliver.
ideas.revenue_model: Lab packages sell at $9-14k against a landed cost of $5-6k. A curriculum and refill subscription adds $600 per school per year. Districts pay a $1-3k decommissioning fee per closure in place of an auction consignment fee, or grant surplus title for free.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A closing school is a fully assembled, curriculum-matched capital asset that public procurement can only sell by the pound, while the same asset is the binding constraint on practical-exam pass rates in low-fee African schools. The margin is in the bundle of equipment, practical curriculum and teacher orientation, not in the equipment, and that bundle is exactly what charity donation programs do not offer.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one district and walk three soon-to-close buildings. Offer free removal of the first 10 science rooms in exchange for title to the equipment. Get letters of intent and 30% deposits from two or three African private-school owners through diaspora, church or school-association networks. Ship one container of two labs plus 200 tested Chromebooks. Line up an export broker and a data-wipe vendor before touching anything.

ideas.title: Savings Groups Finance Apprenticeships via Income-Share
ideas.angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
ideas.one_liner: A mobile-money tool that lets a village savings group use its year-end share-out to pay a workshop for a young member's apprenticeship and starter toolkit, then collect 10-12% of that apprentice's income for two years back into the group.
ideas.customer: Village savings and loan groups, chamas and small SACCOs of 20-30 members in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, which pay the fees. Workshops and TVET trainers who get paid upfront, and employers such as solar installers who want certified graduates, pay referral and placement fees.
ideas.problem: Formal training plus tools costs $150-500, which is out of reach for a household living on irregular farm income. Youth have no credit history. Income-share agreements have mostly failed in rich countries because income verification and collection cost more than the loan. Meanwhile savings groups hold a pile of cash at each year-end share-out and have few productive places to put it.
ideas.solution: A USSD and WhatsApp workflow. The group votes on a candidate. The group pays the trainer in tranches confirmed by attendance and milestone photos. The tool collects a set share of the graduate's mobile-money income into the group ledger, and members receive returns pro rata. Social collateral does the enforcement, so no bureau or aggregator is needed. Legally it is structured as an income-linked group loan, not a security.
ideas.why_now: Sandi AI reports 10,000+ farmer groups across Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania pooling savings for solar irrigation instead of borrowing, so groups will invest pooled money in productive assets. Africa's solar and battery installs are growing about 45% a year and 75% of that is distributed, which creates paid technician work. With six seed rounds for every Series A, outside capital is scarce and group capital is the reachable pool. Reported pressure on Gulf remittances, about $50bn at risk, weakens family-funded schooling.
ideas.revenue_model: A 4% origination fee on training payments, 1% of repayments, and 5-8% referral fees from trainers and tool vendors. Placement fees of about $20 per graduate come from installers and employers. Youth-employment funders can pay $100-200 per verified income outcome, which is what makes the thin margin work at small scale.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The income-share agreement broke in rich countries on enforcement, and a savings group solves enforcement at zero marginal cost because members know the apprentice, the workshop and the family. The year-end share-out also lands in December, right before January apprenticeship intake, so a timing mismatch becomes a built-in cash cycle.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a savings-group promoter NGO or a platform like Sandi AI. Choose five groups within three months of their share-out. Sign three workshops (welding, solar installation, motorcycle repair or tailoring) to milestone-based payment. Launch 10 apprenticeships worth $3-4k, funded by the groups' own money plus a small first-loss guarantee from a grant. Track progress by photo and voice notes on WhatsApp, and record the first income repayments.

ideas.title: Emerging-Market Multigrade Methods for US Microschools
ideas.angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
ideas.one_liner: License and adapt proven low-cost, paper-based, self-paced multigrade teaching systems from Colombia, Bangladesh and India, and sell them as a turnkey kit and training to US microschools and shrinking rural districts.
ideas.customer: Microschool founders and pod networks, including the roughly 1,000 microschools the brief says are in limbo awaiting federal scholarship-credit rules, paying $1,500-5,000 a year. Homeschool co-ops with ESA money and small rural districts forced into combined-grade classes are the next buyers.
ideas.problem: One adult with 6-25 kids across several ages is now the standard microschool model. Guides are often uncredentialed (about two-thirds at Alpha School), 48% of microschool students in one dataset have special needs, and most run on screens. 61% of teachers want less device use, and AI tutors have shown no benefit over plain practice in a two-year Tennessee study.
ideas.solution: Sequenced, printable learning guides for K-6 math and literacy, peer-tutoring routines, student-run classroom governance, a 2-day guide training plus six weekly remote coaching calls, and paper mastery checkpoints. The checkpoints double as evidence for scholarship-granting organizations and ESA administrators. Licence terms give originators such as Escuela Nueva (Colombia), BRAC's one-room schools (Bangladesh) or Rishi Valley's School in a Box (India) a royalty share, so the deal funds their work too.
ideas.why_now: The federal scholarship tax credit starts in 2027 with 31 states opted in and rules still unwritten, so founders are looking for defensible academics. K-12 enrollment is heading from 49.4M to 46.9M by 2031 and more than 1,000 schools closed this year, so multi-age classes are coming to ordinary rural districts. Screen fatigue, AI bans in NYC and LAUSD, and weak AI-tutor evidence all push buyers toward paper and evidence-backed methods.
ideas.revenue_model: A one-time kit plus training at $1,500-3,000 per microschool (about $300 per student), a $600-2,400 annual coaching subscription, and district pilots at $15-40k. Royalties of 10-15% go to the licensors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The US treats one-adult-many-ages classrooms as a Silicon Valley invention. Countries that built them out of necessity decades ago have field-tested materials that are cheap, paper-based, robust to bad connectivity and teacher-light. Those traits match what US buyers suddenly want in 2026: fewer screens, no AI dependence, and documented outcomes. The emerging-market side is the supplier of know-how, not the customer.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact the licensors and negotiate a one-subject pilot licence (grades 2-5 math) in English. Print five paper guide sets. Recruit five microschools through founder communities and networks like the National Microschooling Center at $1,200 each. Record baseline scores with NWEA MAP or i-Ready and re-test after 10 weeks so the results become the first case study.

ideas.title: Warranty-Linked Installer Certification for African Solar Batteries
ideas.angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
ideas.one_liner: Battery and inverter brands pay per certified installer and per registered installation, and every certification requires geotagged commissioning proof, which builds an installed-base registry that lenders and insurers cannot otherwise get.
ideas.customer: Battery and inverter brands and their distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana (and Indian rooftop and backup-power distributors), paying about $8-15 per registered install plus certification event fees. Asset lenders and insurers pay later for registry data. Installers pay $15-25 for the badge.
ideas.problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panel dollars from China since 2024, and 75% of solar growth is distributed. Ember estimates its numbers are 2x the official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Bad installs (loose lugs, undersized cable, misconfigured battery communications) drive warranty costs and fires. Brands cannot tell who installed what and where. Lenders and insurers cannot price the risk.
ideas.solution: A 2-day practical certification in a rented workshop with real inverters, batteries and torque tests, run by senior local installers. After certification, every job requires a geotagged photo checklist and serial scans through a WhatsApp or lightweight app flow, and the brand's warranty desk validates instantly. In return installers get faster claims, brand lead flow and pricing power. Trainees come from underemployed electrical-engineering graduates and, reportedly, technicians returning from Gulf jobs.
ideas.why_now: Africa is installing about 17 GW in 2026 (+45% year on year), with batteries now the larger import dollar. The Hormuz-linked energy shock and diesel costs push more households and shops toward backup power. India's induction-cooktop rush (reported 20-25x demand) is stressing home wiring and backup systems. Official statistics cannot see any of it, so private registries have unusual value.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-15 per registered install from the brand, $1-3k per certification event, and $15-25 badge fees from installers. Lenders and insurers pay $20-60k a year for registry access, or per-lookup fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The certification is the data-collection mechanism. Nobody can sell a registry to a lender directly, but every installer will sign up for a badge that speeds warranty claims, and the registry is exhaust from that. It fixes the exact blind spot Ember describes, and the payer at the start is the brand with a warranty bill, not the trainee.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick Lagos or Nairobi. Sign one distributor of a top-five battery brand as the pilot payer, using its own warranty-claim cost as the case. Rent a workshop and certify 30-40 installers on day one, with the distributor covering $20 per head. Use WhatsApp plus a form tool with serial-number OCR and no custom code. Target 300 registered installs in 90 days and show the brand the change in its claim rate.

ideas.title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Withholding for Sports Tours
ideas.angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
ideas.one_liner: A payout engine for pro-am tours and event organizers that KYCs athletes, collects tax forms, withholds correctly on nonresident winners, files the paperwork, and pays in local currency or stablecoin within 24 hours instead of on a 60-day wire.
ideas.customer: Organizers of tours and one-off events with international fields and $50k-$5M purses: pickleball, padel, fitness racing such as Hyrox, BJJ and grappling, trail ultras, surf and CrossFit-style competitions. Agents and athlete associations are secondary users.
ideas.problem: US-source prize money paid to nonresident athletes is generally subject to 30% withholding unless treaty status is properly documented, with W-8 forms and 1042-S filings. Small organizers mishandle this and carry penalty risk. Athletes wait weeks for wires that cost $25-45 plus FX spread. Athletes in countries like Kenya or Ethiopia often lose another 10-20% to agents, and payments to unbanked winners are a mess.
ideas.solution: A payee vault that holds W-8 and W-9 forms, treaty article claims and sanctions screening. The organizer funds the purse by ACH. The engine applies split rules for sponsor, agent, team and coach, calculates withholding by treaty and state, files 1042-S and 1099 forms, and pays out to bank accounts, mobile money or USDC wallets through partners in supported corridors. Payouts can be triggered at the podium. Each payout also creates a verified earnings record for the athlete.
ideas.why_now: Independent tours and pro-am leagues have multiplied and raised purses through 2024-26. Stablecoins are now regulated plumbing after the GENIUS Act, with the Fed proposing issuer rules on Sept 24, 2026. Circle's $400M Tazapay deal and Yellow Card's $40M raise are building local payout rails in emerging markets. The 1% US remittance tax on cash-funded transfers pushes senders toward digital rails.
ideas.revenue_model: 1.0-1.5% of purse volume, $15-25 per payee onboarding, $10 per 1042-S filed, and an FX spread. A tour paying out $10M a year yields about $150k in revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Sports' payout problem is not moving money, it is proving who is owed what and what to withhold. The rail is a commodity while the compliance file is the moat. Every payout also produces an athlete-verified earnings record, which lets a semi-pro athlete prove income for a bank, visa or insurer, something thin-margin athletes cannot do today.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two fragmented sports with foreign fields, such as a trail-ultra series and a mid-tier pickleball or padel tour. Offer to run payouts for one event at cost. Use a fractional international-tax CPA plus Stripe Connect, Wise or Airwallex for the plumbing. Pre-build a treaty table for the top 30 athlete home countries. Charge 1.5% from the second event onward and aim for five events in 90 days.

ideas.title: Sensor-Priced Insurance for Recovery and Peptide Clinics
ideas.angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
ideas.one_liner: A specialty insurance program that covers contrast-therapy studios, IV and peptide bars and sauna clubs at lower premiums when their sauna, cold-plunge and session logs are streamed as underwriting data.
ideas.customer: Independent and small-franchise recovery studios and med-spa or peptide clinics with 1-5 locations, paying $4-12k a year per location. Excess-and-surplus carriers and wholesalers are the capacity partners.
ideas.problem: Standard general-liability policies exclude or misclassify saunas, cold plunges, IV therapy and peptides. Carriers have no loss history, so operators buy expensive surplus-lines cover. The real exposures are burns, syncope, slip-and-fall, water-quality infections such as Legionella, and unlicensed practice. Franchise growth in recovery is outrunning the insurance market.
ideas.solution: Start as a program manager or agency and grow into an MGA with a fronting carrier and reinsurance. Studios install a roughly $60-250 sensor kit that logs plunge temperature and sanitizer levels, sauna temperature and duration, session counts, waiver and health-screen completion, and staff certifications. A sensor-verified studio earns up to a 25% credit. The program adds an incident-reporting protocol, risk-engineering checklists and, over time, a proprietary claims pool.
ideas.why_now: HHS moved most Category 2 peptides back toward compoundable status in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on July 23, 2026, so peptides are entering clinics and recovery bars without a malpractice rating. Reinsurance is softening, with Jefferies expecting declines through 2027, and record cat-bond and traditional capital means niche programs can find cheap capacity. Recovery studios are among the fastest-growing small-format wellness businesses.
ideas.revenue_model: Commission of 12-15%, an MGA fee of 5-8% of premium, and a profit commission. Sensors and software add $49 a month. 500 locations at $8k premium is $4M of premium and about $700k of revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Underwriters have no loss data on cold plunges and the operators are the only ones who can generate it. A sensor-verified studio is a better risk than a paper-verified one, so the data flywheel is the moat. This is one of the first classes where the insured object, a plunge tank or sauna, can report its own hygiene and temperature.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a retail broker or E&S wholesaler that has a fitness or spa book. Get indicative terms from two E&S carriers on a credit for sensor-verified operators. Recruit 10 design-partner studios through owner communities and sauna or plunge dealer lists, giving them free sensor kits in exchange for logs. Aim for firm quotes within 90 days, and confirm licensing needs with counsel before quoting anything.

ideas.title: Wearable-Triggered Spending Guardrails for Sports Bettors
ideas.angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
ideas.one_liner: A debit card and betting-budget wallet that tightens gambling, day-trading and BNPL limits automatically when the wearer's sleep, heart-rate variability and late-night pattern predict impulsive decisions, with an optional spouse or sponsor as co-guardian.
ideas.customer: US adults who bet legally on sports or prediction markets and want limits: self-referred users, partners and recovery groups first. Credit unions and employer assistance programs are the B2B2C channel. The price is $6-9 a month.
ideas.problem: Roughly 40 states have legal sports betting and sports prediction contracts have spread. Household credit stress is at record levels, with delinquencies at highs and deposits often funded by cards or BNPL. Existing blocks are all-or-nothing, and willpower fails at 2 a.m. after a losing streak. A wearable knows when the user is depleted, but the bank has never seen that signal.
ideas.solution: An issued card and ledger, built on a card-issuing platform, that funds a weekly betting wallet. The user pre-commits the rules when calm. If sleep drops below a set threshold, HRV falls against baseline, or two late-night losses stack up, the wallet enters a 24-hour cooldown, cuts the daily cap, or asks a partner to approve top-ups. Wearable sync is opt-in via Oura, Whoop, Garmin or Apple Health. Only a one-bit cooldown flag leaves the phone.
ideas.why_now: Legal betting and prediction-market sports contracts scaled through 2025-26. Brazil banned online betting and announced debt relief on Sept 25, 2026, showing the politics have turned. The CFPB open-banking rule is stayed and unstable, so a business built on card-level controls avoids dependence on aggregator data. Wearables are now mainstream, with Whoop raising $575M this year.
ideas.revenue_model: $7 a month subscription plus interchange share. Credit unions and neobanks license it for $1-2 per member per month. State problem-gambling councils pay for evidence-based tools. Anything sold to sportsbooks is optional and kept separate to avoid conflicts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Financial products treat every hour as equal, but behavior is not. The best predictor of a regretted transaction is the user's physiological state at 1 a.m., which the user's own wearable measures and the bank never sees. Sell control, not surveillance: the user writes the rules in advance and a bank never sees raw health data.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a no-card MVP: an SMS and Slack bot that uses the Oura or Whoop API to send cooldown alerts, plus a partner-approval flow. Recruit 50 users from recovering-bettor communities. Measure whether cooldowns cut after-midnight deposits. Then pilot with one credit union that already offers gambling merchant-category blocks, and price at $7 a month.

ideas.title: Fitness-Adjusted Longevity Reports for Retirement Advisors
ideas.angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
ideas.one_liner: A report that turns a client's own wearable and clinic metrics (VO2max, resting heart rate, grip strength, gait speed, sleep) into a life-expectancy range for Social Security claiming, annuity timing and withdrawal-rate decisions, sold to fee-only advisors.
ideas.customer: Fee-only RIAs and retirement planners serving affluent pre-retirees aged 58-70, at $75-150 per client report or $300-600 a month per advisor. Later customers are planning-software vendors and annuity carriers.
ideas.problem: Social Security is the largest lifetime asset most households own. Claiming at 70 instead of 62 raises the monthly benefit by roughly three-quarters, and the break-even sits around 80-83. That decision hinges on life expectancy, but planners use population tables. Clients in the top fitness quintile can plausibly outlive the average by several years, and the sedentary can be the opposite. Early claiming reportedly jumped in 2025 amid trust-fund and SSA-staffing fears, so many people are choosing blind.
ideas.solution: Adjust standard actuarial tables using published hazard ratios for cardiorespiratory fitness, gait speed, grip strength and resting-heart-rate trends. Output a range, not a point estimate, showing break-even age versus the chance of reaching it. Data comes in by consented export from Apple Health, Garmin or Oura and is processed locally. The PDF carries methodology and disclaimers written for advisor compliance, and it is explicitly not medical advice or insurance underwriting.
ideas.why_now: Consumer wearables now deliver near-clinical metrics, including FDA-cleared hypertension notifications on Apple Watch in 2025 and VO2max estimates on most premium devices. Basic planning software is being commoditized by AI, so advisors need differentiated inputs. A wave of early Social Security claiming in 2025 shows clients are making irreversible choices under fear. Advisors have avoided health data because of privacy concerns, but client-owned wearable data solves the consent problem.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-report pricing of $75-150, advisor subscriptions of $300-600 a month, and later white-label integrations with planning tools. Annuity carriers may pay for qualified leads.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Planners have been told for decades to plan for longevity risk while seeing only age and sex, and wearables have quietly built the best individual mortality signal outside a hospital. A plus or minus 4-year shift is enough to move the claiming break-even, so precision is not needed. The buyer is the advisor, who needs a fiduciary-safe way to bring health into the conversation.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the calculator from published cohort studies on fitness and gait speed and a standard actuarial table, and have a consulting actuary review it for $3-5k. Run 30 free reports for eight advisors in fitness-forward niches such as physician-focused planners and FIRE planners. Collect feedback and objections. Then charge $99 a report, with no health data stored on your servers.

ideas.title: Per-Class Portable Benefits for Fitness Instructors
ideas.angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
ideas.one_liner: A payout layer that skims a small per-class contribution from studios and class apps into each 1099 instructor's own injury income protection, health-premium credit and retirement account, structured to give studios legal cover under portable-benefits laws.
ideas.customer: Boutique studio groups with 5-30 locations, gym franchisees, class marketplaces and corporate-wellness providers that use 1099 instructors, paying $0.50-2 per class. Instructors opt in for bonus benefits. Trainer associations are a distribution channel.
ideas.problem: Several hundred thousand US fitness instructors and trainers work at 3-6 venues, mostly as part-time or self-employed workers with no disability cover, workers' comp or retirement plan. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired in 2026, federal-marketplace enrollment fell about 21%, and an estimated 4.8M people became uninsured, so self-employed instructors' premiums jumped. Injuries to voices, knees and backs end income immediately. Studios face misclassification suits, and because each studio has separate payroll, no one accumulates benefits.
ideas.solution: Integrate with scheduling systems (Mindbody, Momence, Walla) to read classes taught. Studios contribute a per-class amount into each instructor's benefits wallet, for example $1.25. The wallet buys short-term income protection through a partner insurer, an ACA premium top-up or HSA deposit, and an IRA contribution. Contributions follow the instructor across venues. The structure is designed to fit safe harbors in states that have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 (verify current list and get legal review).
ideas.why_now: ACA subsidy expiry hit self-employed workers in 2026. A handful of states have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 that shield platforms from treating contributions as employment evidence. Class-pass economics keep instructors spread across venues. Misclassification exposure keeps studio owners nervous.
ideas.revenue_model: A platform fee of 8-10% of contributions, insurer commissions of 12-20% on income protection, and interchange on a benefits card. 10,000 instructors at $2,000 a year in contributions is $20M of flow and about $1.6-2M of revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Portable benefits have struggled with gig platforms because work units are messy. Fitness instructors' work is already itemized in software as class events, so a contribution per class is a natural unit. Fitness is the ideal beachhead because work is high-frequency, discrete, multi-venue and tracked, and instructors are health-literate and physically at risk, so they will value injury protection.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one 10-studio group. Run contributions through a simple ACH from the studio. Partner with an existing accident and disability MGA for a $2-4 a week income-protection policy. Enroll 100 instructors and pilot a $1-per-class contribution. Track instructor retention at the studio and first claims. Target 500 instructors within six months.

ideas.title: Robot-Training Disassembly Lab for E-Scrap Magnets
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
ideas.one_liner: A small teardown shop where displaced office workers are paid to take apart hard drives and servers on camera, so sales of robot-training data cover the labor that makes rare-earth magnet recovery uneconomic.
ideas.customer: Two paying buyers. (1) Physical-AI and robotics labs that need real contact-rich manipulation data. (2) Rare-earth processors and ITAD firms that want magnets and boards already pulled out of steel and PCB streams. The workers are laid-off office staff and underemployed recent grads.
ideas.problem: The circular-materials brief says the rare-earth bottleneck is collection and disassembly, not chemistry, and that pulling magnets from hard drives often costs more than the magnets are worth. Robotics labs are short of messy, real-world demonstration data. Meanwhile the expert-gig data economy (Mercor and similar) pays only for screen work, contractors complain of falling pay, and recent-grad underemployment is 42%.
ideas.solution: Rent a bay near an ITAD or data-center decommissioner and take in drives and servers that are already sanitized under NIST 800-88. Workers wear head cameras and instrumented gloves or tool sensors and follow step protocols. An annotation pipeline labels screw types, connectors and failure cases. Sell the licensed video and force data by the annotated hour. Sell the pre-extracted magnet fractions, aluminum and boards to processors. Later, the same corpus trains a disassembly arm that lowers labor cost. Workers earn wages plus a skills log.
ideas.why_now: Physical-AI funding and data hunger are at a peak in 2026. DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic rare-earth supply, and hyperscalers are pushing processors to recover magnets. DRAM prices are up about 400% since early 2024, and data centers turn hardware over every 12-18 months, so teardown yield keeps rising. White-collar hiring is frozen for the young (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are 19% below trend).
ideas.revenue_model: Data licensing per annotated hour (hypothesis to test: $35-60/hr, versus roughly $25-28/hr loaded labor). Materials sales of magnets, aluminum, boards and DRAM/SSD. Per-unit processing fees from ITAD partners. Later, licensing the teardown protocols and a robot-ready dataset.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Disassembly looks unprofitable only because we value just the recovered material. The task has a second output, training data, that has no recovery-cost floor. The uglier and more variable the end-of-life product, the more out-of-distribution and valuable the data is to robotics labs. Recycling's mess is the data moat, and the displaced labor is the cheap input.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one ITAD or decommissioner for a free lot of about 500 sanitized drives. Sign one robotics team for a paid 100-hour pilot. Recruit six workers from laid-off tech and helpdesk groups. Build three capture stations (camera plus glove rig, about $1.5K each). Sell the first magnet and aluminum lot to a local processor to prove the unit economics.

ideas.title: Keep-the-Laptop Severance With Certified Data Wipe
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
ideas.one_liner: At layoff time, employers offer departing remote workers the option to keep their own laptop, remotely wiped and reimaged with a certificate of erasure. The service recovers, refurbishes and resells the devices people don't keep.
ideas.customer: People Ops, IT and Finance leaders at companies running frequent small layoffs of remote and hybrid staff (roughly 10-500 people per round). They buy per device, often through outplacement firms and layoff counsel. The laid-off worker is the beneficiary.
ideas.problem: The 2026 labor market is low-fire, low-hire, so layoffs are frequent and small, and AI is the most-cited reason in Challenger data for five straight months. ITAD firms want pallets, not 40 laptops scattered across 40 homes. Unreturned devices are write-offs and data-exposure risks. Laid-off workers lose their tools just as they must freelance or job-hunt. Candidates are also increasingly expected to own capable hardware and AI tooling.
ideas.solution: On notice day the employee picks Keep or Return. Keep: the device is remotely wiped through the employer's MDM, reimaged clean with an open-source starter kit and optional AI-tool credits, and transferred at appraised fair value, which the employer can subsidize to zero (tax treatment confirmed with counsel). Return: prepaid box, chain-of-custody, refurbish and resell. The employer gets an asset-disposal record, a certificate of data erasure, and a reuse and Scope 3 report. Device-offboarding logistics vendors exist, but they sell shipping. None sells a keep-it option priced as severance.
ideas.why_now: DRAM prices are up about 400% since 2024, so even 3-year-old laptops carry real resale value. Amazon's January 2026 cut of about 16,000 corporate roles and AI-attributed cuts are normalizing rolling layoffs. Breaches such as the Mercor contractor data leak make loose devices a board-level concern. Employers face growing pressure to show soft-landing and circular-IT practices.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-90 per device fee from the employer. Resale margin on returned devices. Upsell of refurbished, warrantied laptop leases to laid-off freelancers. Referral fees from outplacement partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The laptop is the one severance item worth much more to the employee than it costs the employer. It also removes the employer's biggest post-layoff liability, the unreturned device. Small, frequent AI-era layoffs create a long tail of single devices that the pallet-based ITAD industry ignores.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch five HR and IT leaders through outplacement firms and employment-law contacts. Build the flow on existing MDM scripts (Jamf, Intune, Kandji) with a partner ITAD firm issuing certificates. Run a free pilot on one 50-person layoff, then charge about $60 per device. Publish the pilot's unreturned-device rate and cost per device as the case study.

ideas.title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
ideas.one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
ideas.customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
ideas.problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
ideas.solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
ideas.why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
ideas.revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

ideas.title: On-Demand Human Witnesses for Scrap and Recycled Claims
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
ideas.one_liner: A network of trained, insured, credentialed ex-auditors and QA people who can be dispatched within 24 hours to physically inspect scrap lots and witness recycled-content claims, producing tamper-evident signed reports.
ideas.customer: Remote buyers of bales and scrap lots (PET reclaimers, black-mass and tungsten buyers, brokers, traders). Brands making recycled-content claims, and their insurers and lenders. The buyers' own AI purchasing agents consume the reports through an API.
ideas.problem: PET bales trade at a record-low 1.44 c/lb while food-grade supply is called constrained, which points to a quality-tier mismatch nobody can see without inspection. Generative AI makes photos, scale tickets and certificates trivially forgeable. Traditional inspectors have minimum fees and multi-day lead times. Mass-balance claims are contested and no standard exists. California's AB 2253 (claim substantiation) was vetoed, leaving brands exposed to litigation. EU rules banning generic green claims (Directive 2024/825) began applying on Sept 27, 2026.
ideas.solution: Recruit displaced auditors, QA analysts, supply-chain and compliance staff and give them a one-day protocol course on bale and scrap specs. Dispatch them to open and grade bales, XRF-screen metals, seal loads, witness weigh-outs and attend recycled-content production runs. They use a capture app with device attestation and signed provenance, and every report is machine-readable. Visits cost $95-250 versus $800+ for traditional inspection. Each witness builds a portable, scored reputation, so the credential becomes their asset.
ideas.why_now: AI forgery capability is now cheap and widely known, so document trust is falling. The BIS Aug 27 rule adds recordkeeping for black mass and tungsten scrap. Brands need substantiation now that the EU rules apply. Agentic procurement needs verifiable physical inputs. The supply of trained auditors and analysts is growing because of AI-driven cuts.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-inspection fee split about 60/40 with the witness. Monthly claim-assurance subscriptions for brands ($1-3K). API and report-verification fees for buyers' agents. Later, a quality-tier index of bales sold to the market.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When AI can fake any document, the scarce commodity is a credentialed human who was physically present. The scrap trade runs on thin margins and unverifiable quality claims, so cheap, fast human presence beats expensive certification. AI displacement supplies the witnesses at the same moment it destroys trust in paperwork.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one corridor with several bale or e-scrap buyers and offer 20 discounted bale inspections to three remote buyers. Recruit and train 10 witnesses (ex-QA and audit). Build the capture flow on existing attestation and C2PA tools. Publish a first bale-quality report from the results.

ideas.title: Ex-Sales-Rep Route Collectives for Critical-Metal Scrap
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
ideas.one_liner: Commission-only teams of laid-off SDRs and inside-sales reps that each own a territory and sign machine shops and dental and electronics labs to take-back programs for tungsten carbide and cobalt scrap. Lots are aggregated and sold directly to domestic reclaimers.
ideas.customer: Sellers: tens of thousands of small generators such as machine and tool-and-die shops, carbide grinding shops and dental labs. Buyers: domestic carbide and tungsten reclaimers and refiners that now need US-allocated feedstock. Reps: displaced sales staff.
ideas.problem: The BIS rule restricts tungsten scrap exports and the DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic supply, but supply is scattered across small generators who sell to local yards at a steep discount or trash the hard-to-value streams such as grinding swarf. The bottleneck is sales coverage of the long tail, not recovery technology. Entry-level SDR and BDR roles are among the first white-collar jobs AI is absorbing, leaving a large pool of trained cold-outreach talent.
ideas.solution: Each rep owns a metro territory and signs 30-100 shops to a free take-back program: lockable bins, an assay or XRF-based price sheet, payment by lot and simple compliance paperwork (including BIS and toll-processing documentation). Consolidate through partner yards or carriers and sell aggregated lots to reclaimers on term offtake. Start with carbide inserts and grinding swarf, then add cobalt-alloy turnings. Reps keep 15-25% of the net spread and a software backbone handles pricing, pickup scheduling and payouts.
ideas.why_now: The BIS allocation rule created a domestic-first buyer set. Machine shops are squeezed by tariffs and input costs and welcome found cash. SDR and entry-level sales roles are being cut in 2026 and reps are actively looking for commission work. The DOE ($134M) and DoD rare-earth and critical-mineral funding raise buyers' willingness to pay for documented domestic feed.
ideas.revenue_model: Spread on aggregated lots (buy at a fixed percentage of the reclaimer price and sell at the offtake price). Service fee on compliance paperwork. Later, SaaS for yards and reclaimers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In critical-material recycling the scarce resource is neither collection technology nor recovery chemistry but sales coverage of thousands of tiny generators. The people best at long-tail coverage are exactly the ones AI has just made cheap.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one machine-shop-dense metro. Get a reclaimer to sign an offtake letter. Recruit five ex-SDRs and have them call 500 shops from public industrial directories. Collect and sell the first few tons of carbide and swarf, and document real price gaps versus the shops' current yards.

ideas.title: Live-In Caretaker Tenants for Homes in Probate
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A managed service that places vetted short-term tenants in homes stuck in probate. The rent covers carrying costs, the occupied status keeps the house insured, and the estate gets a caretaker instead of a vacant liability.
ideas.customer: Executors and heirs (often out-of-state and aged 50-65), and the probate attorneys, realtors and bank trust officers who advise them. Tenants (traveling nurses, displaced workers, downsizing seniors) pay a reduced rent.
ideas.problem: Probate takes months to a year and a half, and the house sits empty. Standard homeowner policies typically restrict coverage after 30-60 days of vacancy, and vacant-property policies cost far more. Break-ins and burst pipes are common, and the executor pays taxes, utilities and insurance. August 2026 was the strongest buyer's market on Redfin's record (58% more sellers than buyers, 44.7% of sales with concessions), so sales take longer. Meanwhile 20% of renter households paid late or missed rent in 2025.
ideas.solution: Provide a state-specific rolling license or lease template (executor-authority checked by counsel), tenant vetting, an occupied-dwelling insurance rider through a partner MGA, utilities in the caretaker's name, monthly inspections, an inventory with valuables and documents locked away, and a clean turnover at closing. Tenants pay about 70-85% of market rent. The estate pays a flat management fee that is typically below its avoided vacancy costs. The referral funnel is estate attorneys and probate realtors.
ideas.why_now: Rates near 7.5% and record concessions lengthen time-to-sale. The first wave of the wealth transfer is spousal, and hundreds of thousands of homes a year pass through death. Middle-income rent distress is at a series high, and rents are flat nationally, so a discounted, furnished, month-to-month home has a ready tenant pool. AI-armed pro se tenants are a rising risk, which makes well-drafted licenses and vetting a real edge.
ideas.revenue_model: About 10% of rent or a flat $250 per month per house, a setup fee, insurance and utility referral commissions, and an upsell into cleanout, staging and listing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The dead-owner house is the one kind of housing supply that is empty by legal necessity rather than by demand. It stays empty because nobody has authority, insurance or know-how to rent it. Probate delay is a housing-supply constraint disguised as a legal process.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign three probate attorneys as partners. Have counsel draft a license for one state. Recruit about 10 tenant candidates through traveling-nurse agencies, colleges and displaced-worker groups. Get an MGA to quote an occupied rider. Pilot three houses in one county.

ideas.title: Cremation Memorial Rooms in Vacant Office Space
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: Pay-per-event celebration-of-life rooms in empty ground-floor and office space for families choosing cremation, with an optional urn-niche wall run through a licensed cemetery partner as the long-term annuity.
ideas.customer: Families arranging cremation memorials, and direct-cremation providers and independent funeral homes without a venue. Landlords, lenders and special servicers with vacant space earn a revenue share. A licensed cemetery or church partner operates the niches.
ideas.problem: Cremation is about 63% of dispositions and heading to 82% by 2045, so the traditional chapel is redundant, but families still need somewhere to gather and somewhere to keep the ashes. 58% of consumers have attended a service at an unconventional venue, and families pay $2-5K for hotel ballrooms and restaurants. Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally, office CMBS delinquency is 13.2% with $39B maturing within 12 months, and urban cemeteries are out of land.
ideas.solution: Lease or license vacant space on short terms and fit it out as a 40-80 seat memorial room with AV for tribute video, catering and celebrant partners. Sell event packages wholesale to direct-cremation and funeral-home partners and directly to families ($1,500-3,500). In phase 2, add a niche wall sold as perpetual-care niches through a licensed cemetery operator, since a niche needs a fraction of the land of a burial plot. Zoning and state cemetery law vary, so licensing runs through the partner.
ideas.why_now: Cremation crossed 60% and consumer interest in alternatives is rising. Special servicers of distressed office loans will take short-term income from otherwise dead space. Direct-cremation providers are crowded and need a differentiator beyond price. SCI is growing on pricing while volumes fall, which leaves the low-cost end unserved.
ideas.revenue_model: Event fees, wholesale packages for funeral homes and direct-cremation providers, a 10-20% commission or operating share on niche sales, and landlord revenue-share deals. Later, employer celebration-of-life benefits.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Cremation removed the need for the funeral home's most expensive asset, the chapel and its land, but not the human need to gather and to keep remains, which now needs roughly one fiftieth of the space. That makes converted office and retail space, not a cemetery, the right home.
ideas.first_30_days: Get a 90-day pop-up license for a vacant ground floor in a mid-size downtown. Sign two celebrants and a caterer. Offer wholesale rates to five direct-cremation providers and run three events at cost. Meet a licensed cemetery operator to scope the niche-wall pilot and the state licensing path.

ideas.title: Inheriting the Lease: Rent-Stabilized Succession Service
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A service that helps families of rent-regulated elders build and keep the co-residency evidence that lets them inherit a below-market lease, and files the succession claim within days of a death.
ideas.customer: Adult children and relatives living with rent-stabilized or rent-controlled elders (about 1M stabilized units in NYC alone, plus SF, LA, Newark and DC). Elder-law and tenant-rights attorneys, senior centers, home-care agencies and hospital discharge planners white-label or refer.
ideas.problem: In regulated housing, a family member who can prove co-residency (typically 2 years, or 1 for seniors and the disabled) can succeed to the lease. The lease can be worth six figures over time. Landlords, who gain by re-renting at market, often contest, and the outcome hinges on documents families never assembled while the elder was alive (IDs, tax returns, bills, benefit and medical mail). After death the family faces a notice in weeks, with the elder's records locked in an unopened estate.
ideas.solution: Run a lease-inheritance readiness audit and an evidence ledger that collects only genuine documents (address-bearing IDs, filings, bank and medical mail, affidavits from neighbors). After a death, generate a Day-1 succession packet: notice to the landlord, agency filings, and attorney referral. Contested cases go to partner lawyers on contingency or through right-to-counsel programs.
ideas.why_now: NYC's political shift toward tenant protection, the SF rent emergency and record middle-income rent distress raise the stakes. The first Boomer tenants are aging out. Good Cause protections and local rent laws expand the leases worth inheriting. AI-generated pleadings are flooding housing courts, which raises the value of clean, verifiable evidence.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-399 per family file plus $6-9 per month for the evidence ledger. White-label and per-file fees from law firms, nonprofits and home-care agencies. Referral fees from partner attorneys.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For many urban middle-class families the biggest asset passed at death is not money but a below-market lease, and the value is lost through missing paperwork, not through the law. The $124T wealth-transfer statistics ignore it entirely.
ideas.first_30_days: With two elder-law attorneys, draft evidence checklists from the state rent-stabilization rules. Run three clinics at senior centers or tenant associations. Charge $199 for the first 20 pilot families and track landlord responses. Publish a plain-language Succession Readiness Score for tenants.

ideas.title: Funeral Home Land-and-Business Split Advisory
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: An advisor that separates aging independent funeral directors' real estate from their operating business. The land goes to housing developers, the shrunken business is leased back or sold to a consolidator, and the advisor earns fees and a small equity slice.
ideas.customer: Owners of independent funeral homes (about 75% of 15,401 US funeral homes are family or privately owned), especially those over 60 without a successor. Infill housing developers and investors buy the land. Consolidators such as SCI and Everstory may buy the business.
ideas.problem: These sites were built for burial-era visitation: large buildings with big parking lots on prime corridors. With cremation at about 63%, flat deaths and volume down 1.4% at SCI, the buildings are oversized while taxes and upkeep rise. Owners get lowball offers for the business that bundle the land. Developers never see these parcels, which are off-market and not listed. The business buyer pool and the land buyer pool are disjoint and do not talk to each other.
ideas.solution: Screen parcels using zoning, lot size, transit and local cremation share, plus state licensing data on owner age. Offer owners a split: sell or ground-lease the land to a developer and lease back a compact 2,500-3,000 sf service footprint (or a ground-floor space in the new mixed-use building), or sell the business alone to a consolidator. Package parcels for states with single-staircase and missing-middle reforms. Sell paid feasibility studies first, then take closing fees and equity.
ideas.why_now: Single-staircase reform (7 states in 2025, Michigan in July 2026) and California AB 2074 lower infill costs. Rates near 7.5% make greenfield harder, so infill parcels gain appeal. Consolidator cash flow is strong (SCI operating cash flow up 43%), which makes them acquisitive. Cremation growth is making the buildings redundant.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-10K paid feasibility studies, a 2-3% success fee on the land transaction, 5-10% carried equity in the project, and a fee when the business is sold to a consolidator.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Funeral homes are a large class of buildings whose function shrank while owners still think of them as businesses, not real estate. The highest and best use is often housing, and the key is to split the land from the operation so neither buyer pool discounts the other.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull funeral home parcels in two or three states with recent zoning reform. Contact 100 owners aged 60 or over (from state funeral-board license data). Sign three paid feasibility studies. Partner with one infill developer and one consolidator to test appetite.

ideas.title: Inherited Low-Rate Mortgage Concierge for Heirs
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee service that helps heirs keep, assume or transfer a parent's low-rate mortgage instead of paying it off at closing, and values that rate as an estate asset so siblings can buy each other out fairly.
ideas.customer: Heirs (Gen X, aged 45-60) who inherit a home with a mortgage at 3-4% while new loans cost about 7.5%. The estate attorneys, probate realtors and bank trust officers who advise them refer clients and pay for tooling.
ideas.problem: The default estate path is to sell the house and pay off the loan, which destroys below-market financing. On a $300K balance at about 3.25% with 22 years left versus 7.5%, the rate is worth roughly $90K in present value (my calculation). Federal rules generally bar lenders from calling loans due on transfer to relatives at death, and confirmed successors have servicing rights under CFPB rules, but servicers are slow and inconsistent and heirs do not know. Siblings often cannot buy each other out at current rates, and a buyer's market with concessions on 44.7% of sales makes forced sales costlier.
ideas.solution: Within days of a death, verify loan type, rate, balance and assumability and confirm successor-in-interest status with the servicer. Bridge payments during probate, and produce a Rate Asset Report that values the rate for the estate inventory so heirs can split fairly. Structure buyouts with junior notes or partner lenders so one heir keeps or rents the house, and for sellers show where FHA or VA assumability lifts the sale price. Confirm applicability with counsel, since protections generally cover owner-occupied 1-4 unit homes.
ideas.why_now: Rates are rising again (Redfin: futures price the Fed funds rate at 5% by end-2027, and the 30-year is about 7.4-7.6%). A large share of Boomer mortgages sit below 4%, and the first wave of the transfer is arriving. Record concessions make selling into this market expensive. ROAD to Housing Act limits on institutional single-family owners push heirs to be small landlords.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 flat fee per estate or a share of rate-value preserved, a $499 Rate Asset Report, referral fees from buyout lenders, and $200 per month tooling subscriptions for probate attorneys.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The great wealth transfer is counted in balance-sheet dollars, but in a 7.5% world the most valuable asset in many middle-class estates is the interest rate on the parent's mortgage, and the default estate process throws it away at closing.
ideas.first_30_days: Write servicer letter templates and an assumability checklist reviewed by an attorney. Recruit five probate attorneys and three probate realtors. Launch the $499 Rate Asset Report to estates with mortgages and track how many convert to the full service. Sign one HELOC or non-QM lender as buyout-financing partner.

ideas.title: Contingency Water-Bill Recovery for Small Commercial Sites
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office x Water (lens: bookkeeping x utility tariffs)
ideas.one_liner: A no-win-no-fee service that rebuilds small commercial sites' water, sewer and stormwater bills from the local tariff and claws back irrigation-sewer overcharges, leak credits and stormwater-fee errors.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators of small multi-tenant commercial properties (strip centers, 20-200 unit apartment communities, self-storage), churches, private schools and nurseries in cities that bill sewer on metered water and charge stormwater fees. Start in one drought metro. Referral partners are their bookkeepers and property managers.
ideas.problem: A $5k-$40k/yr water bill is too small for utility-audit firms, who chase national chains, and too tangled for the bookkeeper, who codes it and pays it. Tariffs sit in council resolutions. Scarcity tiers and surcharges keep changing. Sewer is often billed on metered water that includes landscape water that never reaches the sewer. Stormwater fees rest on impervious-area estimates that are often wrong. Leak-adjustment windows lapse unnoticed. The Fed's 2026 small-business survey names rising costs the #1 financial challenge.
ideas.solution: The owner forwards bills or connects QuickBooks/Xero and the utility portal. An LLM pipeline reads the tariff PDF and rebuilds every bill. It flags misclassified meters, irrigation on sewered meters, overnight-flow leak periods in interval data, impervious-area disputes (checked against aerial imagery) and estimated reads. A human analyst files the credit, refund or reclassification with the utility, chases it to cash, and writes corrected coding back into the books. Wedge product: an 'irrigation-sewer plus stormwater credit audit' for one metro and three utilities.
ideas.why_now: 49.6% of the US was in drought on Sept 24, 2026 after the warmest June-August on record, so scarcity pricing and surcharges are multiplying. Regulated private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 ($43.5B over the decade) and recover it through rate cases that small customers never see. LLMs make it cheap to read hundreds of heterogeneous tariffs and bills. Customer portals increasingly expose interval meter data. Intuit and Xero are rebuilding around LLM subscriptions and cannot easily take contingency fees.
ideas.revenue_model: 30% of verified first-year savings plus recovered refunds (contingency). Then a $25/site/month monitoring plan that stops corrections regressing and catches new leak periods. White-label for property managers at about $8/door/year.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The one-time refund is the hook, not the product. The value is the permanent reclassification of the account (meter class, irrigation split, impervious area), which lowers every future bill. The moat is a tariff library that human auditors cannot afford to build for accounts this small. Outcome-priced work does not fit subscription incumbents, so the real competitor is nobody.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro with a published stormwater-credit manual and an irrigation or deduct-meter option. Hand-collect five utilities' tariffs. Recruit 20 owners through the local apartment association or BOMA chapter and 5 bookkeepers who get a 10% referral. Audit 24 months of bills per site with the LLM pipeline plus one analyst, with no upfront fee. Targets: 10 audits by day 30, first 3 recovered checks by day 60, then publish anonymized results as the sales asset.

ideas.title: Fractional Operator for Tiny Private Water Systems
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office x Water (lens: compliance and succession x PFAS)
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee compliance back office and operator-of-record for the mobile-home parks, small subdivisions and rural employers that own small water systems and are about to face PFAS testing in 2027.
ideas.customer: Owners of mobile-home parks, small private water companies and HOA systems, and rural employers or private schools with their own wells. These are community and non-transient non-community systems, typically under 3,300 people. The owner is often an aging individual or family LLC with no operations staff.
ideas.problem: Owners face initial PFAS monitoring in 2027 and a 4.0 ppt limit still on the books. EPA's May 2026 proposal would move compliance from 2029 to 2031 and drop limits on four other compounds. The lead action level tightens on Nov 1, 2027. The whiplash freezes capex. Nobody at the business knows the sampling calendar, the accredited lab, the state portal, or the money ($1B of IIJA earmarked for PFAS testing and treatment, $7.2B of FY2026 SRF). The owner also cannot sell, because a first sample becomes a disclosure.
ideas.solution: Wedge: a $1,500 flat 'PFAS-2027 Readiness Pack' covering the sampling plan, lab coordination, result interpretation against 4.0 ppt, state filing and an options memo (treat, interconnect, drill, or sell). Upsell to a $600/mo retainer for the sampling calendar, consumer confidence report, lead inventory, monthly operator logs, tenant submetered billing and bookkeeping for a segregated water fund. The operator-of-record role is subcontracted to a state-certified operator partner. Later, broker and operate systems whose owners want out.
ideas.why_now: EPA's May 2026 proposals to delay PFAS compliance and rescind four limits have left small owners paralyzed, while 2027 initial monitoring still stands. Public money is earmarked: $1B IIJA for PFAS, $7.2B FY2026 SRF, and states are pushing consolidation of non-viable systems. The Boomer ownership wave is hitting the same long tail of tiny systems. EPA's science office was eliminated in 2026, so owners get less federal guidance.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500 Readiness Pack. $400-$900/mo retainer per system by size. 6% success fee on SRF or state grants won. 2-4% brokerage fee on systems sold, plus an option to acquire orphan systems at distressed multiples using consolidation money.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Federal delay does not remove the liability that appears at the first sample. Once a 2027 result exists it becomes a disclosure item in any sale, loan or insurance renewal. So the smart small owner samples early and under a plan. The firm that holds the compliance record becomes the natural buyer of last resort for a long tail of systems too small for the big acquirers. The retainer is the cheapest way to source those succession deals.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one retired state-certified operator as partner and one accredited PFAS lab for a bulk rate. Join two state manufactured-housing associations and the state rural water association. Run free 'is my system covered?' webinars. Sell 10 Readiness Packs at $1,500 in one state, and use the results to prep 3 grant applications. Start compliance-only and add operator-of-record after the partner clears state rules.

ideas.title: Turf-Ban Pivot Desk for Lawn and Irrigation Crews
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office x Water (lens: local marketing x utility rebates)
